title: Distinguish long-pending scans in the review queue
description:
A scan that reaches `awaiting_ocr` and is never confirmed or discarded stays there for good. That is the right answer to what to do with it — it is unfinished work, and deleting somebody's photograph because they got busy is not the application's call — but "kept forever" and "kept and forgotten" are different outcomes, and the queue currently delivers the second.

The queue shows pending scans in one undifferentiated list. A scan from this morning and a scan from four months ago read the same, so the old one is not so much waiting as lost, and the person who took it has no way to notice it without scrolling to the bottom of a list that only grows.

## Shape

Show age where it changes what a person would do. A scan old enough that its taker has plainly moved on is worth marking, and worth being able to filter to, so the queue can be worked down deliberately rather than only from the top.

What "old enough" means is a display threshold, not a deletion threshold, so it can be generous and it costs nothing to be wrong about. It belongs beside the retention setting the scheduled sweep introduces rather than as a second unrelated constant.

The affordance that matters is not the badge, it is being able to act on the group: reaching the old ones, seeing them together, and discarding the ones that are genuinely abandoned. Discarding is what makes them eligible for the sweep, so this is the path by which stale scans actually leave, and it puts the decision with the person who took the photograph.

## What this is not

Not an expiry, not a nag, and not a default filter that hides old scans. Something a person has not finished should stay visible; the point is that they can tell which is which.

## Tests

Unit: the threshold reads from configuration; a scan either side of it is classified correctly; the queue's ordering does not change.

E2e: the queue distinguishes a recent scan from an old one, filtering to the old ones shows only those, and discarding from that view removes the scan from the pending queue.

title: Add a full-record view showing MARC source and otzar's own metadata
description:
A record detail page shows the fields a reader needs. There is no way to see everything otzar holds about a record, and no way to see the MARC it was built from.

Two audiences want this. A cataloguer evaluating whether otzar read a record correctly needs the source next to the interpretation. Anyone debugging an ingest or a match needs the fields that drive scoring and identity, which are deliberately not on the reading view.

## What it shows

**otzar's own metadata**, the values held but not displayed: normalised forms used for matching, the source catalog and the query that found the record, the cascade step that matched, confidence or score values, external identifiers (VIAF, ISSN, control numbers and their authority-file prefixes), timestamps, and the fields recording how a work relates to a set.

**The MARC source**, as retrieved. Field tag, both indicators, and every subfield with its code, in record order. Indicators and subfield codes have to be visible: the parsing work turns on 490 first indicator, on 830 $w and $x, on 245 $n and $p, on 880 $6, and on whether 040 $e names a description convention. A view that renders subfield values as running text hides exactly what matters.

Offer the raw MARCXML too, for copying into a bug report or a validator.

## Notes

Not every record has MARC behind it. Records created from a scan and OCR have no source record until a candidate is confirmed, so the MARC half needs an empty state that says which of the two applies.

Records vary enormously in size, from a dozen fields to well over a hundred with linked 880 pairs. The layout needs to stay usable at both ends, and 880 fields read best next to the field they are linked to rather than in tag order at the bottom.

Access is a question to settle when it is built: the MARC source is not sensitive, but otzar's internal scoring values are closer to debugging output than to catalog content.

title: Let an unnumbered series hold more than one volume
description:
`SeriesVolume` declares `unique_together = ("series", "volume_number")` with `volume_number` a non-null `CharField`. A series statement carrying no `$v` normalizes to the empty string, so the empty string behaves as a volume designation that exactly one record per series can hold.

Confirming a candidate now links it to its series, which makes this reachable. The first volume of an unnumbered set takes the empty position; every later volume of the same set is logged at WARNING and left with no series position. A twelve-volume set catalogued from records that carry `490 $a` without `$v` ends up with one volume attached and eleven unattached.

The constraint is right for numbered volumes: two records both claiming volume 3 of one set is a real conflict worth surfacing rather than resolving silently. It is wrong for the empty string, which is not a position but the absence of one.

Fix: make `volume_number` nullable, store NULL rather than "" when the source gives no designation, and replace `unique_together` with a `UniqueConstraint` conditioned on `volume_number__isnull=False`. Rows excluded by the condition are not in the index, so unnumbered volumes stop colliding while numbered ones keep the guard. Needs a schema migration plus a data migration for existing "" rows.

Check the series detail page and `create_series_volumes` against a null designation before landing. `SeriesVolume.Meta.ordering` is `["volume_number"]`, so the unnumbered volumes will collect at one end of the list and the page should say what they are rather than showing a blank cell.

comments.author: dchud
comments.text: Absorbed into bd-tz2s.3. The empty-string collision is the narrow symptom; the ticket it belongs to is the one deciding what a volume's position means when no source supplied one. Landing the constraint fix on its own means a migration that work would immediately migrate again.

title: Retire the historical planning documents in docs/plans
description:
`docs/plans/` holds four documents totalling ~2,500 lines. Three of them describe work that has since landed, and the convention now is that plans are working artifacts that get deleted once the work is done rather than kept as standing design documents.

They are also the only part of the tree exempted from `scripts/lint_process_labels.py`, because they are dense with bead IDs, PR references and time-state wording. Retiring them narrows or removes that exemption.

## The four

`extract-from-experiments.md` (159 lines) — a one-off migration plan for pulling experimental code out of `../learn/z3950`. The migration happened. Nothing references it.

`implementation-plan.md` (947 lines) — a phased handoff written for an implementation team that turned out to be one person. Its phases are built.

`app-plan.md` (364 lines) — the original application plan. Largely implemented; whatever design rationale in it is still live belongs in `docs/` proper or in a bead, not in a plan.

`long-term-plan.md` (1,027 lines) — different from the other three. It is a July 2026 review plus a forward plan, written deliberately and merged recently, and it is the only one describing work that has not happened yet.

## Shape

For the first three: confirm nothing in `docs/` or the README links to them, extract any design rationale that is still true and not recorded elsewhere, then delete them. Git history keeps them.

`long-term-plan.md` needs a decision rather than a default. Either it stays as the living roadmap — in which case the lint exemption stays for that one file and it should be kept current — or its forward-looking content becomes beads and the file goes. The second is more consistent with tracking work in one place, but it is a real loss of narrative that beads do not carry well.

Once the directory is empty or down to one file, tighten `EXCLUDED_PATHS` in `scripts/lint_process_labels.py` accordingly.
close_reason: done

title: Clear expired sessions on the deployed host
description:
Sessions use the database backend (`otzar/settings.py` sets no `SESSION_ENGINE`), and Django removes expired rows only when `manage.py clearsessions` runs. Every visitor who enters the site password gets a session row (`SitePasswordMiddleware` sets `site_password_ok`), as does every login and every QR handoff, and nothing runs `clearsessions`. `django_session` therefore grows without bound, and every row goes into the Litestream replica and the snapshots.

Run `docker compose exec app python manage.py clearsessions` daily from a host timer installed by the provisioning script, beside the snapshot timer and the staging sweep.

Tests: N/A, the command is Django's. On the instance, confirm the timer is listed by `systemctl list-timers` and a run exits zero.

title: Review queue visibility for non-staff catalogers
description:
`review_queue` in `ingest/views.py` filtered pending scans to `scanned_by=request.user` unless the user is staff, and `confirm_scan`, `discard_scan`, the title-page endpoints (`run_ocr`, `edit_title_metadata`, `discard_title_scan`), and the helpers behind confirming and re-searching a scan (`_close_scan_for_record`, `_scan_for_repeat_search`, `_in_progress_title_scans`) applied the same rule. The workflow the project describes, several people scanning while one reviews, worked only when the reviewer held the staff flag, which also grants the admin. bd-nzb carries the same, now-unscoped, count into the queue item on the ingest mode bar.

Decision: every logged-in cataloger sees and can act on the whole pending queue. The `scanned_by`/`is_staff` gate is dropped from `review_queue`, `confirm_scan`, `discard_scan`, the three title-page endpoints, and the three private helpers listed above; `@login_required` is the only access control left on them. A queue for a circle of friends does not need per-user privacy, and dropping the filter kept the change small. The alternative, a reviewer role separate from staff (a Django group and a permission check in place of `is_staff`), is the shape a multi-catalog server would need, not this one.

`scan_poll`, the desktop poll pane that shows a barcode scan arriving from a paired phone, keeps its unconditional `scanned_by=request.user` filter. It never had a staff exception and it isn't a review surface -- it's the live view of one cataloger's own capture session, and the pending queue's visibility decision doesn't reach it.
close_reason: done

title: Stop calling the OCR path Claude Vision
description:
"Claude Vision" appears fourteen times across five files, referring to a product that does not exist. No Anthropic product carries that name. The OCR path calls the Messages API with image input.

| File | Occurrences | Shape |
|---|---:|---|
| `ingest/ocr.py` | 7 | Module docstring and six log messages |
| `docs/development.md` | 4 | Running prose, twice naming the module |
| `README.md` | 1 | The three-ways-in list, in the first screen a reader sees |
| `docs/user-guide.md` | 1 | Running prose |
| `docs/administration.md` | 1 | A section heading |

The name matters more than a naming nit usually would, for two reasons.

These documents are the only place a reader learns what the application sends to a third party, what it costs, and what an API key is for. Somebody who searches for "Claude Vision" pricing, rate limits or model names finds nothing, or finds something unrelated and wrong.

And the documentation is published now, so this is a public-facing error rather than an internal one. `README.md` is the first screen anyone reads, and `docs/` renders as a site with the same name in a section heading.

## What to replace it with

What actually happens: the Anthropic Messages API with image input, or simply "the OCR call" where the transport is not the point. Name a model only where a specific model is meant, and prefer pointing at the `CLAUDE_MODEL` setting over naming one in prose, since prose does not track a default.

`ingest/ocr.py` carries seven of the fourteen, and six of those are log messages. Those are what an administrator reads while debugging a failed scan, so they are worth the same care as the prose — a log line naming a product that cannot be searched for is the same failure in a less visible place.

## What to leave

`docs/plans/` uses the name in several files. Those are working artifacts recording what was believed when they were written, and are exempt from the persistent-artifact rules.

`docs/development.md` also says tests "hitting Claude Vision" require a live API key. The suite blocks sockets, so that sentence is doubly wrong, but the second half belongs to whoever revisits how the OCR tests are described rather than to this change.
close_reason: done

title: cleanup_staging sweeps tmp/title_pages while staged images live under media/staging
description:
`ingest/management/commands/cleanup_staging.py` deletes `discarded` ScanResults older than the retention period, then removes old files from `BASE_DIR/tmp/title_pages/`. That directory was the staging area before the title-page handoff; uploads go to `ScanResult.image` under `MEDIA_ROOT/staging/YYYY/MM/DD/` (`staging_image_path` in `ingest/models.py`), so the orphan sweep reads a directory nothing writes to.

Point the sweep at `MEDIA_ROOT/staging/` and define an orphan as a file no ScanResult references that is older than the retention period. Deleting a ScanResult row through the ORM does not delete its file, so delete `scan.image` on the rows the command removes as well; discarding a title scan already deletes the file at discard time, so this covers rows discarded by other paths and files whose delete failed.

otzar-eiy proposes a separate command for stale `awaiting_ocr` rows. Fold it in here as a second criterion with its own threshold rather than adding a second janitor. Update the `cleanup_staging` section of the administration guide.
close_reason: Merged in PR #50

comments.author: dchud
comments.text: When rewriting the sweep, go through the storage API (default_storage.listdir and delete) rather than os.listdir: under bd-n7a media moves to S3 (bd-n7a.2), and a directory walk finds nothing there.

title: Add K10plus as a lookup source
description:
K10plus is the German union catalog (the GBV and SWB merger), serving MARC21 over SRU at https://sru.k10plus.de/opac-de-627 with no key and no registration. It holds 113,379 Hebrew-language records, against 14,158 at DNB.

## Why this source rather than simply another one

K10plus is one of only two catalogs of five that populate leader/19, multipart resource record level — the MARC position declaring whether a record describes a set, a part carrying its own title, or a part whose title depends on the set. It is coded on 24% of K10plus book records and on 14% of DNB's, and on one record between LC, NLI and Oxford combined.

That is where set membership is actually recoverable. Treating "773 present and 245 $n or $p present" as a test for a declared dependent part scores precision 1.000 and recall 0.996 against leader/19 across K10plus and DNB: 272 true positives, no false positives, one miss. The same test matches none of the 2,620 book records held by LC, NLI and Oxford. Those catalogs do not merely leave the distinction undeclared — they do not express it in the fields either.

So this is not one more source of candidate records. It is one of the two available sources whose records can establish that a volume belongs to a set at all, and the larger of the two.

The supporting measures agree. Among book records K10plus carries 773 on 35% (LC: none at all), 245 $n or $p on 18% (LC and NLI: 1%), and monographic component parts on 16%. In a four-way comparison of one book's series it was the only catalog of four to supply the series ISSN, and one of two to supply $w links to the series' own bibliographic record.

It is not a substitute for DNB. DNB is the national deposit library; K10plus is the union catalog of the academic libraries, and it carries the collections that matter here — Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin and Frankfurt UB. The two overlapped on twelve ISBNs in the survey corpus, the largest overlap of any pair, so expect duplicate candidates and let scoring resolve them.

## Confirmed by probing

Indexes that answer: `pica.isb` (ISBN), `pica.spr` (language), `pica.slw` (subject), `pica.jah` (year), `pica.all` (keyword). Boolean `and` works. `startRecord` paging works. `recordSchema=marcxml` returns MARC21.

Not yet probed, and the first task here: the title, publisher and place indexes the cascade needs. The Pica index set does not use the `dc.` or `alma.` names, so `K10PLUS_CASCADE` cannot be adapted from either existing cascade by substitution — the index names have to be established against the server first.

## Where it goes

**ISBN lookup.** `isbn_lookup` already fans out to NLI, LC and DNB and merges the results; adding a fourth arm with `pica.isb` is one query and the smallest useful increment. Worth doing first and on its own.

**Title cascade.** Needs its own `K10PLUS_CASCADE` and `search_k10plus`, following the shape of the existing two.

**Reading the result.** Whatever consumes these records should read leader/19 where it is present. It is the one place in the corpus where the set relationship is stated rather than inferred, and it is absent from every other source otzar queries.

## Ordering

Every source runs on every lookup and the candidates are pooled for scoring, so ordering is not a short-circuit decision — it decides latency and the order results appear in `cascade_info`. Put K10plus after NLI and LC, which are the highest-yield sources for this material, so the first results a user sees are the most likely matches.

The cost is real and worth stating: each source adds its cascade steps multiplied by the inter-request delay to every scan. If that budget becomes a problem, the honest trade for this material is to keep K10plus over DNB rather than to run both, on the evidence above.

## In the deployment

Read the endpoint from `SRU_K10PLUS_URL` with the public URL as the default, as `sources/sru.py` does for NLI, LC and DNB, and list it in `.env.example` and the configuration table in `docs/administration.md`. Add `sru.k10plus.de` to the outbound check bd-n7a.4 runs from AWS before provisioning. In the deployment each lookup runs inside a request on one of eight threads, so the added steps cost thread time as well as latency: a K10plus arm that times out holds a thread for 30 s per step.

title: Rework the review queue into scannable rows with inline confirm
description:
The queue shows a candidate count and hides everything else behind a
Details button at the far right of each row. Deciding whether a scan
matched the right book means clicking through, and the expanded view
then offers "Use this" with little more to go on.

`_candidates.html` -- written for the title-page cascade results --
already renders the layout this needs: title/author, date,
publisher/place, series, identifiers, source, one row per candidate.
The queue's `_queue_item.html` predates it and duplicates none of it.

## Shape

Extract the candidate row markup from `_candidates.html` into a shared
partial and render it in the queue, so both surfaces stay in step.

Clicking a row expands it in place (Alpine is already in this template)
to show the full field set the record would receive -- subjects,
additional authors, identifiers, language, series -- with a Confirm
button inside the expanded row, so the decision and the action sit
together.

Each row also carries a "See full record" link that POSTs the candidate
JSON to `select_candidate`, which already stores it in session and
redirects to `/ingest/confirm/`. That is the same review page the
title-page results reach, so the queue stops being the one path that
commits without a preview. No new view is needed.

## Zero-candidate scans

A scan with no candidates currently says so only behind Details. Those
rows should say it at the top level and offer an action -- re-run the
search, or discard -- rather than expanding into an empty box.

## Prerequisite, already landed

Both confirm paths now build records through
`_create_record_from_candidate` (commit 8b4b6ca), so the inline Confirm
and the review page produce identical records. That had to come first;
before it, the queue path silently dropped `source_marc` and any date
that would not parse as an integer.

## Testing

E2e for expand-in-place, inline Confirm, and See full record reaching
`/ingest/confirm/`. The record-equivalence unit tests already exist.
close_reason: Merged in PR #30

title: Convert the remaining markup-coupled locators in end-to-end tests
description:
`tests/e2e/` holds 103 locators built from a CSS class, an id or an attribute selector, against 34 built with `get_by_role`, `get_by_label` or `get_by_text`, across 16 files. Each of the markup-coupled ones asserts that a particular piece of markup exists, which is a fact about the templates rather than about what a person can do, and this rework renames a great deal of what they bind to.

The convention for new tests is written down in `CLAUDE.md` under "Locators in browser tests". This is the retrospective half, deliberately left until the screens stop moving: converting a locator before the redesign renames its target means editing the test twice, and a test edit that changes no behaviour is hard to review and easy to get subtly wrong.

## They are not all the same problem

**Styling classes.** `.btn-idle`, `.btn-busy`, `h2.text-xl`, `ul.text-sm li` — Tailwind utilities standing in for meaning. These are the clear wins and the ones the rework is most likely to break. The busy state already has a semantic answer: the button carries `hx-disabled-elt`, so `to_be_disabled()` reads it.

**Ids that exist to be styled or scripted.** `#upload-btn`, `#isbn-input`, `#capture-error`, `#viewfinder`, `#results`, `#search-controls`. Most already have an accessible name or role to reach for instead — `#capture-error` carries `role="alert"` today and the test binds to the id anyway.

**Ids carrying a primary key.** `#title-page-card-{scan.pk}` (17 uses), `#scan-{pk}-candidate-{n}`, `#scan-{pk}-row-{n}` — around a third of the total. These are the hard case and they are not a smell: role and label cannot distinguish one queue row from an identical row beside it, and the test genuinely needs to say *which*. The answer is a `data-testid` carrying the key rather than an `id` doing double duty as a style hook, so restyling cannot break a test and a test cannot pin a selector the stylesheet wants to change. Doing this well means deciding the attribute naming once and applying it across the queue, candidate and card partials together.

## Where the markup is the actual problem

A control a test cannot name by role or label is usually one a screen reader cannot announce either. Every locator in the second group is worth reading as a question about the template before it is read as a question about the test: is this control missing a label, a heading level, or a role? The conversion is worth more for what it forces into the open than for the test hygiene.

## Tests

The suite passing before and after is the whole acceptance criterion — no behaviour changes here. Convert a file at a time so a regression is bisectable, and do not mix a locator conversion with a behaviour change in one commit.

title: Image decode failure leaves the capture form dead and silent
description:
`_title_page_form.html` wraps `createImageBitmap` in a try/catch that
logs to the console and returns. The Upload button stays disabled and
the preview stays hidden.

The user taps "Take title page photo", picks an image, and nothing
happens on screen -- no error, no indication the tap even registered.
Reachable with HEIC on Firefox, or any corrupt capture.

Surface the failure, and consider falling back to submitting the
original file unresized rather than refusing it: the resize is a
bandwidth optimisation, not a requirement.

Found in review of PR #7.
close_reason: Merged in PR #17

title: Set survey: hand-labeled ground truth, generated tables, and a checkable definition of done
description:
The set survey in the cataloging-practice study has regressed twice while being corrected. Every number in it is produced by filters in `set_report.py` that have no ground truth to be scored against; the only oracle has been a reviewer reading raw records, which is slow, covers only what the reviewer opens, and gives no signal when a fix breaks something it did not touch. The last regression anchored the title filter at the start of `245 $a`, which dropped 488 records beginning "Sefer …", reported zero K10plus records for Ein Yaakov while the response held records titled "Sefer ʿEn Yaʿaḳov …" coded as dependent parts, and printed an em dash for the National Library of Israel's holdings of Miqraot Gedolot, which sit in `245 $b`. Separately, every figure in the eight chapters is hand-typed, so each filter change cascades into manual edits and transcription errors, and "done" has meant "the reviewer found nothing", which does not terminate.

This epic ends the cycle with four things. A hand-labeled validation set, drawn from the records the catalogs returned rather than from what the filter accepted, so both precision and recall are measurable. A labeling tool that shows the raw record and nothing derived from it. Tables and inline numbers generated from data and included by the documentation, with a lint that fails on any hand-typed figure and a claims script that fails when regenerated numbers no longer support an interpretive sentence. And a definition of done that a script can check.

The labeled set serves two purposes and the second matters more. First, it validates the three filters: is this record an edition of the work asked for, is it a monograph, is it library-created or publisher-supplied. Second, it gives ground truth for the study's actual question: does this record describe a whole multi-volume set, one volume of a set, a single-volume resource, or something else. With that, the study can report how well each catalog signal (set-level extent, leader/19, 773, 245 $n/$p, 505) predicts an expert judgment, instead of reporting only that the signals correlate with one another. That table becomes the survey's main result.

Scope is bounded. One vocabulary revision is allowed after the pilot; two filter revisions are allowed against the bar; if the filter still misses the bar, the study reports the labeled sample directly with stratum-weighted estimates and intervals, and the filter is demoted to sizing the population. Each of those branches terminates.

## Definition of done, all checkable

1. `labels.jsonl` holds at least 800 main-pass records with every stratum in the sampling plan filled to target, plus at least 80 holdback records relabeled after seven or more days.
2. Intra-rater agreement on the holdback is Cohen's kappa at or above 0.80 for the level label and 0.90 for the relation label, or the vocabulary was revised once and the holdback relabeled, whichever came first.
3. On the labeled set, the relation filter has precision at or above 0.95 and stratum-weighted recall at or above 0.90 for "edition", overall and in each catalog with at least 40 labeled records; the vendor flag has precision at or above 0.95 and recall at or above 0.90; the monograph filter has precision at or above 0.98 — or the fallback was invoked and is stated in the limits.
4. `scripts/lint_study_numbers.py` passes: no digit-bearing token in the prose of `docs/practice-study/*.md` outside code spans, years, MARC identifiers, and `references.md`, except generated tokens.
5. `studies/cataloging-practice/claims.py` passes against the committed `numbers.json`.
6. Running the pipeline twice from the frozen data produces no git diff in `docs/practice-study/`.
7. `./scripts/check.sh` is green, including the existing process-label, wrap and orphan-footnote checks.
8. Every SVG figure was written by the same pipeline run that wrote the tables it sits beside, and figure text is text.

## Effort

Engineering: frame and sampler one day, tool one day, scoring and filter revision one to two days, generated tables, hook, lint and claims one to two days, docs rewrite one day; about five to seven working days.

Labeling: pilot of 150 records, two to three hours including learning the tool; full pass of 650 more at 45 to 60 seconds each, twelve to fourteen hours in sessions of no more than ninety minutes; holdback relabel of 80, one hour. About fifteen to eighteen hours in total.

## Is it worth it

The pilot is worth doing unconditionally: 150 labels would have caught every regression so far and takes an afternoon. The full pass is worth doing only if the set survey stays a headline chapter or the signal-versus-judgment table is wanted as a published finding. If neither, stop after the pilot, keep the short survey section, close the epic through the fallback, and report the pilot sample's rates with their wide intervals. The decision point is the pilot task.

Interim recommendation: do not hold the pull request for the corpus chapters, which have held across four review passes. Cut `sets.md` to the qualitative pattern and the two hand-verified contrasts, mark the survey tables as pending this epic, and merge.

title: Interim: cut the set survey to what does not depend on the filter
description:
Reduce `docs/practice-study/sets.md` to what holds without the filter chain: the correspondence pattern stated qualitatively; the two contrasts verified record by record (Entsiḳlopedyah talmudit, two LC records with open-ended extents against thirty-one K10plus volume records; Encyclopaedia Judaica); the statement that leader/19 is coded only at the two PICA catalogs and set-level extents appear only at the three Anglo-American ones; and the known failure modes of the current filter, named. Remove the work-by-work table, the per-catalog percentage table, the era-stability section and every percentage derived from `set_report.py`. Keep the "How good is this evidence" section, shortened.

Update the cross-references in `index.md`, `signatures.md`, `markers.md`, `cases.md`, `implications.md` and `data.md` that quote survey numbers or the four-idioms framing, and remove the stale sentences the fourth review listed: "contains almost no volumes of sets", "held by at least three", "1,180 records examined", "converge completely", "all four mechanisms". Mark `set-survey.csv` in `data.md` as provisional pending this epic.

Done when the practice-study pages build, the process-label and wrap checks pass, and no sentence in `sets.md` states a number that came from `set_report.py`.

title: Generated tables and numbers: render script, MkDocs hook, snippets, lint, claims
description:
Mechanism. `studies/cataloging-practice/render_tables.py` reads `final_stats.json`, `confidence.json`, `set_summary.json` and `labels_scoring.json` and writes every table in the eight chapters as a Markdown fragment under `docs/practice-study/tables/`, each beginning with a comment naming the script and the input file, committed to the repository. Chapters include them with the `pymdownx.snippets` block syntax, which ships with Material for MkDocs; enable it in `mkdocs.yml` if it is not already on. The same script writes `docs/practice-study/data/numbers.json`, a flat map of every inline figure the prose cites, keyed by chapter and name.

Inline numbers. Add a MkDocs hook, `docs/hooks/numbers.py`, registered under `hooks:` in `mkdocs.yml`, that replaces `{{num:key}}` tokens in page Markdown from `numbers.json` and fails the build on an unknown key. No plugin dependency. Prose that cites a figure writes the token, never the digits.

Interpretive prose. A sentence like "set-level extents appear on most LC records and on almost none at the PICA catalogs" keeps its words and cites its tokens; the threshold that makes the words true is asserted in `studies/cataloging-practice/claims.py`, one assertion per interpretive sentence, reading the committed `numbers.json` — for example `lc.set_level_pct >= 50`, `pica.set_level_n <= 6`, `anglo.l19_coded == 0`. A failing assertion fails the build. Sentences whose claim cannot be written as an inequality are rewritten until it can, or dropped.

Absence is rendered distinctly: a generated cell shows "0 of 50 returned" rather than an em dash when a query returned records and the filter accepted none, and the dash only when nothing was returned. That ambiguity is what made the National Library of Israel appear not to hold Miqraot Gedolot.

Lint. `scripts/lint_study_numbers.py`, run by `check.sh`, fails on any digit-bearing token in the prose of `docs/practice-study/*.md` outside code spans and generated includes, except four-digit years, MARC tags and positions, footnote markers, and everything in `references.md`. The allowlist is a regular expression in the script, not a per-line exemption comment.

Conversion. Convert all eight chapters and the figure captions. Figures are regenerated by `charts.py` in the same pipeline run with `svg.fonttype` set to none.

Done when the lint passes on the converted chapters, `claims.py` passes, `mkdocs build --strict` passes, and a deliberate change to one value in `set_summary.json` propagates to every table, token and claim that depends on it with no manual edit.

title: One-command pipeline and the regeneration gate
description:
Add a Justfile recipe `study` (or `studies/cataloging-practice/run.sh`) that runs, in order: `featurize.py`, `final_stats.py`, `set_report.py`, `score_labels.py`, `render_tables.py`, `charts.py`, `claims.py`, `scripts/lint_study_numbers.py`, `mkdocs build --strict`. `analyze.py` and `confidence.py` are slow and run behind a `--full` flag; their outputs are inputs to the renderer and are committed. The recipe refuses to run without the corpus and says where the archive is.

Gate: running the recipe twice on the frozen data must leave `git status` clean under `docs/practice-study/`. That is the local definition of "the documentation is the data". `check.sh` does not run the recipe, since it needs the corpus, but does run the lint and `claims.py` against committed files, so a hand edit to a number or a stale claim fails CI.

Update the study README: the order, the gate, the labeling tool and its tests, and `frame_counts.json` as the labeled population. Remove the sentence saying the scripts are kept as they ran; from this task on they are the pipeline.

Done when the recipe runs end to end, twice, with no diff, and `check.sh` is green.

title: Rewrite the set chapter and data page around the labeled results
description:
Rewrite `docs/practice-study/sets.md` in this order: the correspondence pattern in ground truth (per-catalog base rates of whole-set, volume and single labels among editions); the signal-versus-judgment table, which is the chapter's result; the filter scores, stated as the survey's own quality control; the record-count contrasts; then leader/19 as the sharpest encoding, stated as encoding rather than measurement, with the era section reduced to a paragraph. Every table is an include and every figure a token.

State the single-rater limitation, the kappa, the masking of leader/19 during labeling, and that the expert label is a reading of the record, not an inspection of the item.

Update `data.md`: add `set-labels.csv` with a column dictionary naming `sha256` and `retrieved` and saying the file is joinable to a fresh fetch on catalog plus 001, the frame counts, the sampling strata and weights, and the guide version; note that the labels carry record identifiers only. Update `implications.md` so each practice that rested on survey numbers cites tokens, and `index.md` so pattern 1's strength is restated from the labeled evidence.

Done when the chapter builds from includes and tokens only, the lint and claims pass, and the fourth review's stale-sentence list has no survivors.

title: Build the frozen candidate frame from the survey responses
description:
Write `studies/cataloging-practice/frame.py`. It recomputes each survey query's cache key with the same logic as `sru_fetch.fetch` (no network; every response is cached), parses every record the 110 queries returned, deduplicates within a catalog on `001` while keeping the list of works whose query returned the record, and writes `tmp/vagf/frame.jsonl`: one line per record with `record_id` (`catalog|003:001`), `catalog`, `works_returned_for`, `retrieved` (the cache file's date), `sha256` of the MARCXML as retrieved, the full MARCXML string, and the current pipeline's outcome computed by importing the functions in `set_report.py` — title accepted or not, leader/07, vendor flag, extent class, leader/19 value, 773, 245 $n/$p, 505 presence. The pipeline outcome is stored for stratification and scoring only; the labeling tool never reads it.

Also emit `tmp/vagf/frame_counts.json`: records returned, deduplicated, and per stratum as defined in the sampling task, so the sampling plan can be sized from real counts rather than estimates. Expected order of magnitude: about 4,100 response records, somewhat fewer after deduplication, of which about 1,500 are currently accepted.

Done when `frame.jsonl` round-trips (every record parses; every record in `set_summary.json` is present) and `frame_counts.json` is committed to the study README as the population the labels were drawn from.

title: Label vocabulary and labeling guide
description:
Write `studies/cataloging-practice/label/GUIDE.md`, the only document the labeler reads. It defines five fields per record, each a single keypress in the tool, plus a confidence flag and a note. One vocabulary revision is permitted after the pilot; after that the guide is frozen and the version is recorded in every label.

`work`: which of the 22 works the record describes, or `other-work`, or `none`. Chosen from the list, not typed.

`relation`, with respect to the chosen work: `edition` — the described resource's main content is the text of the work, in any language, whole or part, with or without commentary, including translations, abridgments and selections; `about` — a study, index, concordance, bibliography, review or commentary that stands without the text; `unrelated` — the title matched but the resource is something else (children's books under ספרי). `none` under `work` implies `unrelated`.

`level`, the study's question, judged from the whole description: `whole-set` — the record describes a multi-volume resource as one thing, whether or not the extent counts the volumes and whether or not the set is complete; `volume` — the record describes one physical volume, or a small numbered subset, of a multi-volume resource, whether or not it is linked to a parent; `single` — one physical unit that is not part of a set, including one-volume editions of a multi-volume work; `analytic` — a part smaller than a volume: a tractate within a volume, an article, folios in a codex, a track; `other` — archival collection or subunit, serial, kit, collection-level e-resource.

When `level` is `volume`, a sixth field `own-title`: `standalone` if the volume's title would identify it without the set title, `dependent` if not, `unsure`. This is the property leader/19 `b` and `c` encode, labeled without seeing the code.

`origin`: `library` — created or adapted by a library, including copy cataloging; `vendor` — publisher- or aggregator-supplied, typically an e-book record with a 776, a vendor code in 040 $a, or a batch-load signature; `unsure`.

`carrier`: `print`, `online`, `other`. Labeled separately from `origin` so the "online resource" heuristic can be scored as a heuristic.

Uncertainty: every field carries `sure` or `unsure`; an unsure label still records the best choice. `cannot-judge` is a value for `relation` and `level` only, reserved for records too sparse to read (no 245, or a 245 that is only a number); it is not a synonym for unsure and is expected on under two per cent of records. The note field is free text and is required when `cannot-judge` or `other` is chosen.

The guide includes twelve worked examples drawn from the frame, at least three of them Hebrew-only records and two of them the "Sefer ʿEn Yaʿaḳov 5" and "Ḥamishah ḥumshe Torah … Miḳraʾot gedolot" shapes that the current filter misses, with the correct labels and the reason. Examples are excluded from the sample.

Done when the guide covers every field, every value, the uncertainty rule and the examples, and the tool's option keys match it.

title: Stratified sampling with a seeded draw, holdback and pilot
description:
Write `studies/cataloging-practice/label/sample.py`. It reads `frame.jsonl`, assigns each record to one stratum from the pipeline outcome, draws with a fixed seed, and writes `tmp/vagf/sample.jsonl` with the stratum in a field the tool never displays.

Strata and targets, per catalog unless stated. S1, currently accepted library records: 80 per catalog, 400 total, allocated across works proportionally with a floor of two per non-empty catalog-work cell, and within each catalog balanced across three predicted level classes (set-level extent present; leader/19 coded or 773 or $n/$p present; neither) so predicted negatives for the level question are labeled. S2, vendor-flagged: all of them. S3, title-accepted but not leader/07 `m`: all of them. S4, title-rejected records carrying any set signal (set-level extent, leader/19, 773, or 245 $n/$p): 40 per catalog, 200 total, or all if fewer; this is where the costly misses live. S5, title-rejected with no set signal: 20 per catalog, 100 total. Total about 800.

Justification. Precision of the accepted set at an expected 0.95: 400 labels give a Wilson half-width near two points overall and five per catalog. The "0 coded" claim for the Anglo-American catalogs: 240 accepted Anglo labels at zero errors give a 95% upper bound of about 1.2%. Recall of the title filter: misses are concentrated in S4; 200 labels there bound the per-catalog miss rate within about ten points, which combined with S1 decides whether recall clears 0.90. Signal versus judgment: LC's set-level extent at an expected precision near 0.9 needs about 100 LC set-extent records for a five-point half-width, which the S1 allocation supplies.

Order and holdback. The output order is a seeded shuffle that interleaves catalogs and strata and never places two records of the same work consecutively, so no run of similar records anchors the labeler. Ten per cent (80 records), drawn across strata, are flagged `holdback` and are served again in a fresh shuffle in the relabel pass no earlier than seven days after the main pass. The pilot is the first 150 records of the shuffled order. Stratum weights (population size over sample size) are written to `tmp/vagf/sample_weights.json` for the scoring script.

Done when the sampler is deterministic under its seed (a test), every stratum meets its target or exhausts its population, and the guide's examples are excluded.

title: Labeling tool: local web page over the sample, raw record only
description:
Build `studies/cataloging-practice/label/serve.py` and `label/index.html`. Recommendation: a local web page served by the Python standard library, not a CLI and not part of the Django application. Web because the records mix Hebrew and Latin script inside one field and terminals mis-render mixed-direction lines; a browser with `dir="auto"` and `unicode-bidi: isolate` on each subfield value renders them correctly, and a fixed layout with keyboard shortcuts is faster for thirty-field records. Not Django because there are no models, no users, no migrations and no deployment; it reads and writes files under `tmp/vagf/` and must run with zero setup. No Tailwind build, no CDN: one HTML file with inline CSS and plain JavaScript, so it works offline and does not depend on the application's toolchain. It lives with the study scripts because it is research tooling and is excluded from the linter like the rest of the directory.

Display, per record: the catalog name; the leader as a raw string with position 19 masked (it is the encoded form of the very judgment being labeled; everything else in the record is description a cataloger legitimately reads, and the masking is stated in the docs); control fields raw; every data field as `tag ind1 ind2` followed by subfields with codes visible, each value in its own bidi-isolated span; a monospace font with Hebrew coverage. Never displayed: the query, the stratum, the filter's verdict, the pipeline flags, any derived classification, the pilot or holdback status, and during the relabel pass the earlier label. Progress is shown as a count only.

Rendering lives in `studies/cataloging-practice/label/marc_html.py`, a module with no imports beyond the standard library. Its input is a plain record structure — `leader` string, `controlfields` as (tag, value) pairs, `datafields` as (tag, ind1, ind2, [(code, value), ...]) — built by a separate ten-line function from the frame's MARCXML; its output is the HTML for one record, plus a constant holding the CSS block. Masking is the caller's job, done on the structure before rendering, so the renderer never knows what leader/19 is. The module's docstring states the five rendering rules (visible codes, one span per subfield, `dir="auto"` with `unicode-bidi: isolate`, tag and indicators as a prefix, monospace with Hebrew coverage) as a contract. This is the one piece written so it can be lifted: the application's full-record view and any later record-comparison view can move the file into `catalog/` or `sources/` unchanged and wrap it in a template tag, feeding it records from mrrc rather than from XML. No shared package is created now, the application does not import from the study directory, and no Django template is written until a consumer exists.

Interaction: single-key choices for each field in the guide's order, `u` toggles unsure on the current field, `n` focuses the note, Enter saves and advances, Backspace returns to the previous record for correction. Each save appends one JSON line to `tmp/vagf/labels.jsonl`: `record_id` (with `catalog`, `003` and `001` also as separate fields, never a row number), `pass` (`main` or `holdback`), every field and its confidence, the note, `seconds` measured from render to save, an `idle` flag when a gap over five minutes was observed, the guide version, and a timestamp. Append-only; on start the tool skips records already labeled in the current pass, so a session can stop at any record and resume. A `--pass holdback` flag serves the holdback records in a new shuffle.

Tests beside the tool under `label/tests/`, run explicitly and named in the study README; not wired into `check.sh`, because the studies directory is outside the application's gate by decision and these tests must never depend on scratch data. Three things get tests because a fault there silently corrupts the ground truth: the renderer emits every subfield code and never emits any string from the pipeline-outcome fields or the word "stratum"; append, resume and holdback logic never loses or double-serves a record; the sampler is deterministic.

Done when the author has labeled ten guide examples in it end to end, the three test groups pass, and a session interrupted mid-record resumes at that record.

title: Pilot: label 150 records and decide
description:
The author labels the first 150 records of the shuffled sample in sessions of no more than ninety minutes. Then run the scoring script on the pilot only and record four things in this bead: median and 90th-percentile seconds per record, split Hebrew-only versus other; the share of `unsure` and `cannot-judge` per field; the pilot's filter precision and recall with intervals; and any field where the labeler found the guide ambiguous, with the records concerned.

Decision, recorded here. If a field's unsure rate exceeds 20% or the labeler reports ambiguity, revise the guide once, bump the guide version, and relabel the pilot records whose field changed meaning; this is the one permitted revision. Then decide whether to proceed to the full pass. Proceed if the set survey is to remain a headline chapter or the signal-versus-judgment table is wanted as a finding. Otherwise stop here: the pilot's 150 labels become the labeled set, the scoring script reports them with their wide intervals, and the epic closes through the fallback with the short survey section as the published form.

Done when the four measurements and the decision are in the bead and, if proceeding, the full-pass estimate is revised from the measured seconds per record.

title: Full labeling pass and holdback relabel
description:
The author labels the remaining records of the sample to the stratum targets, in sessions of no more than ninety minutes, with the `idle` flag left to mark interruptions. No earlier than seven days after the last main-pass session, the author relabels the 80 holdback records in the relabel pass without seeing the earlier labels.

Budget, to be revised from the pilot: about 650 records at 45 to 60 seconds each, twelve to fourteen hours; holdback one hour. If the measured pace is worse than 90 seconds per record, reduce S5 to ten per catalog and S1 to 60 per catalog before reducing anything else, and record the change in the sampling script.

Done when every stratum meets its target or exhausts its population, the holdback pass is complete, and `labels.jsonl` validates against the guide version.

title: Scoring: filters against labels, signals against judgment, rater consistency
description:
Write `studies/cataloging-practice/score_labels.py`. It joins `labels.jsonl` to `frame.jsonl` and `sample_weights.json` and writes `tmp/vagf/labels_scoring.json` and the published `docs/practice-study/data/set-labels.csv` (record identifiers and labels only, no record content).

Filter scores, overall and per catalog, with 95% Wilson intervals on precision and stratum-weighted estimates for recall (misses in S4 and S5 scaled by their stratum weights): relation filter for `edition`; leader/07 `m` filter against `level` in whole-set, volume, single; vendor flag against `origin`; the "online resource" heuristic against `carrier`. Confusion matrices for each.

Signal scores, the study's result: for each of set-level extent, leader/19 `a`, leader/19 `b` or `c`, 773, 245 $n/$p, and 505, precision and recall against `whole-set` and against `volume`, per catalog, restricted to labeled editions of the works; and leader/19 `b` versus `c` against `own-title`. Report the base rate of each level label per catalog on the same table, since that is the one-record-or-thirty finding stated in ground truth.

Rater consistency: Cohen's kappa per field on the holdback, plus the raw agreement and the count of changed labels; the median seconds per record overall and for Hebrew-only records; unsure and cannot-judge rates.

`set-labels.csv` carries `sha256` and `retrieved` beside each label, so a later consumer fetching the record afresh can tell whether the catalog has changed it since it was judged, and is joinable to a fresh fetch on `catalog` plus `001`.

Every number the scoring writes carries its `n`, and the scoring output is the sole source for the survey tables from here on.

Done when the script runs on the pilot, its output round-trips into the generated tables task, and the kappa computation is tested against a hand-computed two-by-two case.

title: Revise the filters against the bar, or invoke the fallback
description:
Bar, from the epic: relation filter precision at or above 0.95 and stratum-weighted recall at or above 0.90 overall and per catalog with at least 40 labels; vendor flag precision at or above 0.95 and recall at or above 0.90; monograph filter precision at or above 0.98. At most two revisions of `set_report.py` are permitted, each re-scored against the same labels, and each recorded in this bead with the before-and-after scores. Because the labels were read after the current filter was written, the first revision may use them freely; the risk is fitting the filter to the sample, which is why the count is two and why the holdback is scored separately.

Known directions for the first revision, from the reviews: match 245 $a and $b together; allow an optional leading "Sefer", "ספר", "Sefer ha-" or "Ḥamishah ḥumshe Torah" before the anchored name; keep the Sifre constraint; treat leader/07 `a` and `d` as rejections before title matching so articles never count; make the vendor rule a conjunction of carrier and 040 $a or 776 rather than the extent string alone.

Fallback, if the bar is not met after two revisions: the survey reports the labeled sample directly — stratum-weighted rates with intervals for each catalog and signal — and the filter is used only to size the frame. The generated tables switch to the scoring output as their source with no change to the documentation build, and the limits section states which bar was missed and by how much. This branch terminates the epic as fully as the other.

Done when either the bar is met and recorded, or the fallback is recorded and the tables point at the scoring output.

title: Split the survey's eras on cataloging history, and on the right date
description:
The survey in `docs/marc-in-practice.md` splits records into eras at 1945 and 1990. Those are dates in the history of the world rather than dates in the history of cataloging, and the split is on the wrong field besides.

## Two dates, and they are not the same

MARC `008/07-10` is the date the *book* was published. MARC `008/00-05` is the date the *record* was created. In this corpus they are far apart: the median gap is 19 years, and 274 records of 973 were catalogued fifty or more years after the book was printed. A pre-war book catalogued in 1990 carries 1990's practice, not 1914's.

Splitting on both and comparing shows they explain different fields, which is the finding worth building the section around:

| Field | By publication date | By record-creation date |
|---|---|---|
| `020` ISBN | 0% → 29% → 47%, a clean step | 9% → 25% → 33%, smeared |
| `264` RDA publication | 4% → 9% → 18% → 79%, gradual | 1% → 2% → 58%, a sharp break |

An ISBN is a property of the book, so its presence follows when the book was printed. RDA encoding is a property of the cataloging, so it follows when the record was made. Reporting one date for both hides the mechanism in each case.

## Boundaries worth using

Anchor them on things that changed cataloging, and say in the text what each one is, so a reader can check the claim rather than take the boundary on faith:

- ISO 2108, 1970, which made the ten-digit ISBN an international standard after the nine-digit SBN was used in Britain from 1967. Nothing published before it can carry one except by later reprinting.
- ISO 3297, 1975, for the ISSN, which is why the series ISSN is scarce here beyond its scarcity for monographs.
- The thirteen-digit ISBN, mandatory from January 2007, which is checkable directly: the ratio of `978`-prefixed to ten-digit values should turn over at that date.
- AACR2, published 1978 and implemented by LC in 1981.
- RDA, published 2010 and implemented by the national libraries in March 2013, which is when `264` starts replacing `260`.
- Retrospective conversion, running through the 1980s and 1990s, which is the reason the two dates diverge so widely and the reason an old book can carry a modern record.

Verify each date rather than taking it from this ticket, and cite it in the document so the boundaries are arguable.

## What to do with it

Report the field table against both dates where they disagree, and say which one explains the field and why. Where they agree, one table is enough. The point is not more granularity for its own sake; it is that a reader deciding whether to parse a field wants to know whether its absence tracks the book or the record, because only one of those is a thing a collection can be described by.
close_reason: done

title: Configure Dependabot with a cooldown and grouped updates
description:
There is no `.github/dependabot.yml`. Dependency updates happen when somebody notices, which means they arrive in batches, as large diffs, at moments nobody chose. The refresh that pinned ruff is the worked example: an upgrade nobody had been tracking turned into 89 lint findings across 24 files and a rule-set decision that needed its own ticket.

Two ecosystems apply. `uv` covers `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock`. `github-actions` covers `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, which pins `actions/checkout`, `actions/cache` and `astral-sh/setup-uv` by tag. There is no npm manifest — the Tailwind CLI is a downloaded standalone binary, not a package.

## What it has to do

**A cooldown of seven days.** A release that is yanked, or hot-fixed two days later, should never become a pull request. For a catalog maintained by one person the cost of being a week behind is nothing; the cost of a pull request for every point release is attention, which is the scarce thing here.

**Grouping by update type, per ecosystem.** Patch and minor updates arrive as one pull request per ecosystem. Major updates stay separate, because a major is a thing to read rather than a thing to merge, and burying one inside a group of eleven patches is how it gets merged unread.

**A cap on open pull requests**, so a quiet fortnight does not produce a queue.

Dependabot's `cooldown` and `groups` configuration keys cover all of this. Check the current schema when writing the file rather than copying a remembered shape; both features are recent enough that the key names have moved.

## What this project should expect from it

The lint gate is now ruff's default rule set, and `uv.lock` is what pins the ruff that defines it. So a ruff bump is not a dependency change: it can move the rule set and surface findings in files nobody touched. That is the intended behaviour and the reason the pin was replaced by a lockfile pin, but it means a ruff pull request should be read as a possible code change and is worth separating from the group that carries everything else.

The same holds for Playwright, where a browser build can change what the end-to-end suite sees without any test changing.

## Verification

CI runs on Dependabot pull requests unaffected: the test gate skips only `.beads/*` and `*.md`, so a lockfile change runs the full suite. Confirm that on the first pull request rather than assuming it.

A grouped update lands as one pull request with the group name in the title, and a major update for a package inside that group arrives separately.
close_reason: done

title: Rehearse the deployment locally with the real image and deploy files
description:
Rehearse the whole deployment on the owner's machine before anything is provisioned in AWS. Everything except Lightsail, the firewall and DNS can be exercised locally, with the real image and the real `deploy/` files, and a fault found here costs a restart rather than a cloud bill or a half-built instance.

## Shape

`deploy/compose.local.yml`, run by `just rehearse up|down`:

- the app, from the image built locally from the current commit with `GIT_COMMIT` set, and the same `compose.yml` settings as production (fixed network, bind-mounted `DATA_DIR` under `./tmp/rehearsal/`, log rotation);
- moto in server mode (the `motoserver/moto` image; moto is already the suite's S3 stand-in) as both buckets, created on start with versioning on, reached through `AWS_S3_ENDPOINT_URL`. Its state is in memory and lasts as long as its container, which covers a rehearsal session; the rehearsal restarts the app container, never the moto one, when it tests a restore. MinIO is not used: its community repository was archived in 2026 and ships source only. If a durable local store is ever needed, SeaweedFS is maintained and speaks S3;
- Caddy with the production `Caddyfile` and `tls internal` in place of Let's Encrypt, on `https://otzar.localhost`, so the proxy headers, the secure cookies, the request size cap and the maintenance import run as they will in production;
- an `.env` produced by `just configure --local`, which fills the same template with local values.

## What it has to show

Each item is run and its result written down in the PR:

- A first start on an empty data directory creates an empty database and replicates it: LTX objects appear under the replica path in the stand-in bucket.
- A title page uploaded through the browser lands in the media bucket, and its presigned URL loads in the browser.
- The site password gate stands in front of the login pages, and logging in works behind it.
- `snapshot_db` writes a snapshot, a manifest and `latest.json`, and a stale replica makes it report failure.
- `just rebuild --latest`, `--at` a few minutes earlier, and `--snapshot` each restore the expected record count, and each switches replication to a new path while leaving the old one intact.
- `deploy.sh` run with a second commit installs a changed `Caddyfile` and reloads Caddy.
- `just maintenance on|off` shows and clears the 503 page, and `/health/` stays up while it is on.

The Lightsail-specific parts (provisioning, the firewall allowlist, the burst alarm, the IAM policy's address condition) are not rehearsable here and stay with bd-n7a.4 and the production smoke test.

## Tests

The rehearsal is itself the test; unit and e2e are N/A. Keep it runnable: after the first deploy it remains the way to try a change to `deploy/` before shipping it.

title: Title-page scans never leave pending after a candidate is chosen
description:
Photograph a title page, run OCR, search catalogs, pick a candidate: a
Record is created and the ScanResult stays `status="pending"` with
`ocr_output` set, forever.

`title_page_poll` shows `pending` rows that have output, so the card
reappears in the "Incoming photos" pane on every device on every poll
tick, and sits in `/ingest/queue/` permanently. The pane fills with
scans that are already catalogued.

The link is dropped in the round trip. `_ocr_results.html`'s search form
posts only the metadata fields to `title_page_upload`; the response,
`_candidates.html`, has a "Use" button that posts to `select_candidate`
-> `confirm_candidate`. Nothing in that chain knows which ScanResult the
metadata came from, so nothing can mark it confirmed.

Carry `scan.id` through the search form and the candidate form, and set
`status="confirmed"`, `created_record`, and
`selected_candidate_index` when the record is created --
`confirm_scan` already does exactly this for the queue path.

Found in review of PR #7. P1 because every successful title-page ingest
leaves permanent debris in the one pane the workflow depends on.
close_reason: Merged in PR #7

title: Put the login pages behind the site password gate, and let the QR handoff through
description:
The deployment runs with `SITE_PASSWORD` set, and the gate in `SitePasswordMiddleware` (`otzar/middleware.py`) is the outer lock on the site: the one check a stranger can reach, so it has to be cheap and it has to stand in front of everything expensive. Today it stands in front of the wrong things.

## The login pages sit outside the gate

`EXEMPT_PATHS = ("/admin/", "/accounts/", "/health/")`. A stranger can go straight to `/accounts/login/` or `/admin/login/` and post guesses without ever seeing the gate. Each guess costs a PBKDF2 hash (1.5M iterations; about 0.1 s of CPU on a laptop, several times that on a Lightsail vCPU, which is burstable and throttles to its baseline once its credits run out) and, on failure, a django-axes write to SQLite that Litestream then replicates. axes locks a username at an address; it does nothing about a run that rotates either. A few guesses a second hold both vCPUs.

The gate's own check is a constant-time comparison with no database write on failure. Putting the login pages behind it means that only someone who already holds the shared password can reach the hash, and axes goes on protecting each account behind it.

Remove `/admin/` and `/accounts/` from `EXEMPT_PATHS`. A cataloger's first visit becomes: the gate, the shared password, the login page, their own password. After that they are authenticated, which passes the gate, and a session lasts two weeks.

## Logout keeps the gate open

Logout flushes the session, and with it `site_password_ok`, so a cataloger who logs out meets the gate again on their next click. The shared password is not what logging out is meant to revoke. Log out through a `LogoutView` subclass that sets `site_password_ok` on the new session when the old one had it.

## Accepting the password must redirect

When the right password is posted, the middleware sets the flag and passes the same POST on to the view underneath. The view receives a submission meant for the gate: the login view shows "Invalid username or password", and a GET-only view returns 405. Answer an accepted password with a 303 redirect to the same path and query string, so the page underneath loads with a GET.

## The QR phone handoff has to pass

`/ingest/phone-auth/<token>/` is opened by a phone with no session, so behind the gate the phone gets the password prompt before `phone_scan_auth` runs. The signed token is itself the authentication: a `TimestampSigner` signature with a one-hour `max_age`, logging the phone in as the user who generated the code. Exempt `/ingest/phone-auth/`. No other `/ingest/` path needs it: every other ingest view requires login, and a logged-in user passes the gate.

`/health/` stays exempt for the uptime check.

## The gate has to be on

With `DEBUG` false and `SITE_PASSWORD` empty, every page and both login forms are open to anyone, and nothing says so. Add a Django system check that reports a warning in that case, so `manage.py check --deploy` and the container's startup output name it. A warning rather than a refusal: a public catalog is a legitimate choice, it is just not the one this deployment makes.

## Rotation

Changing the shared password is a change to `.env` and a restart; every session that passed the old gate keeps its flag until it expires. `docs/administration.md` says so, and says how to end those sessions at once (`manage.py clearsessions` removes only expired ones; deleting all sessions logs everyone out).

## Tests

Unit, with `SITE_PASSWORD` set: a fresh client on `/accounts/login/` and on `/admin/login/` gets the gate, not the form; a POST of credentials to `/accounts/login/` without passing the gate does not reach authentication (no axes attempt recorded, no hash computed); the right site password on `/accounts/login/?next=/ingest/` answers 303 to that same URL; a logged-in user who logs out can load a gated page without re-entering the site password; a valid phone-auth URL logs a fresh client in and redirects to the scan page; an expired or tampered token still returns 403 or 400; another `/ingest/` path still gets the gate; the system check warns with `DEBUG` false and no `SITE_PASSWORD`, and not otherwise. E2e, with `SITE_PASSWORD` set: a cataloger passes the gate, logs in, logs out and logs in again without the gate reappearing; a second browser context opens the QR URL and lands on the scan page.

title: Vendor HTMX and Alpine.js instead of loading them from unpkg
description:
`templates/base.html` loads HTMX 2.0.4 and Alpine.js 3.14.8 from unpkg.com. Every page that uses HTMX polling or Alpine state (the scan pages, the queue, dark mode, the ingest mode bar) depends on a third-party CDN being reachable from the browser, and cataloging happens at the shelves on whatever wifi is there. When the script fails to load, the page renders and the interactivity does not, with no error a user sees.

Copy the two files into `static/js/` with the version in each filename, reference them through `{% static %}` with the same `defer`, and let WhiteNoise serve them as it serves the stylesheet. Note the versions in the development guide so an upgrade is a file replacement. Add a test that no template references an external script host.

title: Image decode failure leaves the capture form dead and silent
description:
`_title_page_form.html` wraps `createImageBitmap` in a try/catch that
logs to the console and returns. The Upload button stays disabled and
the preview stays hidden.

The user taps "Take title page photo", picks an image, and nothing
happens on screen -- no error, no indication the tap even registered.
Reachable with HEIC on Firefox, or any corrupt capture.

title: Stop embedding full candidate records in the results page
description:
`ingest/views.py` pairs each candidate with `json.dumps(c)` and `_candidates.html` writes that into a hidden `<textarea name="candidate_data">` on every row, so the entire candidate list — including everything the parser extracted — ships to the browser and comes back on submit.

Adding `source_marc` to parsed records grew this roughly ninefold: about 4.4 KB of MARC per candidate, taking a 20-candidate results page from 12.7 KB to 111 KB. An ISBN lookup hitting NLI, LC and DNB could reach roughly 300 KB. The page works, and this is not urgent, but the growth is structural: every field the parser learns to extract makes the page heavier, whether or not the browser needs it.

## Shape

The server already has what it needs. `ScanResult.candidate_records` holds the list and `confirm_scan` already selects by index, so the round trip could carry `(scan_id, candidate_index)` instead of the record itself, and `select_candidate` could read the candidate server-side rather than parsing it back out of the form.

The obstacle is that not every path into `_candidates.html` has a ScanResult to key off — check `isbn_lookup_view` and the title-page cascade search before assuming. If one path genuinely has no scan, that path can keep the embedded form and the common case can still be fixed.

Coordinate with bd-73m, which reworks the review queue and extracts a shared candidate row partial from this same template. Do this after that lands, not alongside it.

Compression (see the response-compression bead) reduces the symptom by about 85% and is a much smaller change; do that first and reassess whether this is still worth doing.

title: Run the staging sweep on a schedule with a configured retention period
description:
`cleanup_staging` removes discarded scans and orphaned staging images, and an administrator runs it by hand. The user guide describes it that way because it is true, but it is not what the application should offer: the images are photographs taken inside someone's home, shop or synagogue, and how long they sit on disk after being discarded should not depend on whether anybody remembered to run a command.

Run the sweep on a schedule on the deployed host, and make the retention period a setting rather than an argument, so the schedule and the window are configured in one place instead of the window living in a cron line.

## Where it belongs

The host and its provisioning script are the deployment work, so the timer belongs there rather than in the application: a systemd timer or a cron entry calling the management command with `--apply`, installed by the same script that provisions the instance.

Running it inside the web process was considered and rejected. An opportunistic sweep on a request path does irreversible deletion during somebody's page load, at a time nobody chose, and it makes the retention promise depend on traffic.

## What the schedule has to get right

Deletion is not reversible and the command knows it, which is why it reports by default. A scheduled run passes `--apply` and therefore skips that safety, so its output has to go somewhere a person can read after the fact — the run's log, retained long enough to answer "what happened to my scan".

A failed run must be visible. A timer that silently stops firing turns a stated retention period back into a fiction, which is the state this ticket exists to leave behind.

## What the user is told

Once the sweep is real, the user guide says the period rather than saying an administrator decides. It should read the configured value rather than repeating a number that a setting can contradict, and the place a person is most likely to want it is beside the discard action itself.

## Tests

The command already has its own tests. What is worth testing here is the setting: the retention period is read from configuration, an unset value falls back to the documented default, and the value the user guide surfaces is the value the sweep uses.

## On the deployed host

On S3 a delete is not an erasure. The media bucket keeps noncurrent versions for 30 days and the instance key cannot remove versions, so a photograph the sweep deletes stays recoverable in the bucket for 30 days afterwards. The period the user guide states is the retention setting plus that window; either say both, or give `staging/` a shorter noncurrent expiry in the provisioning script.

The two discard paths differ: `discard_title_scan` deletes the photograph at once, and `discard_scan` keeps it for the sweep. The user guide's paragraph on discarding describes only the second; rewrite it for both.

The orphan half of the sweep does nothing on S3 until `cleanup_staging` goes through the storage API (bd-n7a.2). Scheduling it before then schedules a no-op.

The retention period is `STAGING_RETENTION_DAYS` in the environment, default 30, listed in `.env.example` and the configuration table; `--days` stays as an override for a manual run. Failure is reported the way the snapshot reports it: the command pings `STAGING_SWEEP_PING_URL` on success and the same URL with `/fail` on failure, and bd-n7a.4's alerting section lists it as a fourth check. The timer runs `docker compose exec`, so the run's output is in the host journal (`journalctl -u <unit>`), not in the container's rotated `json-file` log.

title: Edit multiple authors, publishers, locations and subjects in the manual entry form
description:
`RecordForm` in `ingest/forms.py` carries one author (name and romanized name), one publisher (name and place), one location, and no subject field. The models are many-to-many. A record with two authors or two shelf locations can be entered only through the admin, and subjects cannot be added or corrected outside the admin at all, which is where a cataloger ends up for every book with a translator or an editor. The same form serves `/ingest/edit/<id>/`, where `edit_record` shows only `record.authors.first()` and its siblings; check what the save path does with the relations the form cannot show before changing the form.

Turn the single fields into repeatable rows (Alpine for add and remove, a formset or a JSON list on the server side) for authors, publishers and locations, and add subjects with an autosuggest against existing headings in the style of the language field. Keep the authority check working per author row. E2e: enter a record with two authors and a subject, and see all of them on the record page and in search.

title: Decide which of ruff's newer default rules to adopt
description:
The dependency refresh pinned `[tool.ruff.lint] select`, which reproduces the rule set ruff 0.15.9 enabled by default. Without it the upgrade to 0.16.6 reported 89 findings across 24 files nobody had touched, because ruff's implicit default grew from 62 enabled rules to 416.

Pinning was the right call for a dependency PR — it keeps a linter upgrade from becoming a code-change PR — but it defers a decision rather than making one. The pin now states the project's rule set explicitly, which is an improvement regardless; the question is whether that set should stay where 0.15.9 happened to leave it.

## Already decided

`I` (isort) was adopted in the same PR and is not part of this decision. It was never in ruff's default set, so the pin did not drop it; enabling it ratified what the tree already did, and a canonical import order makes the merge conflicts parallel work produces in shared modules resolve mechanically. Seven files were fixed automatically.

## What remains: the 89 findings

Roughly 72 are `RUF012` (mutable class attributes should be annotated `ClassVar`), which lands almost entirely on Django model `Meta` and admin classes — arguably noise for this codebase, since Django's own idiom is a bare list.

The rest are a mixed handful worth looking at individually: `BLE001` (blind `except Exception`), `S112` (`try`/`except`/`continue`), `B017` (assert on bare exception), `TRY401` (redundant exception object in `logging.exception`). Several of those point at real habits in the ingest and sources code, where broad excepts around network calls are deliberate but not always narrowed as tightly as they could be.

## Shape

Go through the categories rather than the 89 individual findings, and decide per rule: adopt and fix, adopt with targeted `noqa`, or leave out of `select` with a comment saying why. Ending with an explicit list that says what this project checks for is the deliverable; a clean run under someone else's defaults is not.

Do this as its own change, not folded into other work — it touches many files shallowly and would drown a review.
