title: Keep subject subdivisions and dedupe repeated headings
description:
The ingest confirm page shows the same subject twice.

`sources/marc.py:210-216` keeps only the first `$a` of each 650 field
and discards the subdivisions (`$v $x $y $z`), with no deduplication.
That produces visually identical entries two ways, both routine:

- Subdivided headings collapse. `650 _0 $a Jews $z Israel $x History.`
  and `650 _0 $a Jews $x Social life and customs.` both emit `Jews`.
- Parallel vocabularies repeat. LC records carry an LCSH `650 _0 $a
  Judaism.` alongside a FAST `650 _7 $a Judaism. $2 fast`; the `$2` is
  invisible here, so the list holds the heading twice.

Reproduced against a synthetic LC-shaped record: five 650 fields yielded
`['Jews', 'Jews', 'Judaism.', 'Judaism.', 'Jews']`.

The visible duplication is display-only -- `get_or_create(heading=...)`
collapses equal headings and the through table has a unique index, so no
duplicate rows exist. The real defect is underneath it: two distinct
headings are both stored as the broad subject `Jews`. The intended form
joins subdivisions with " -- ", as `load_test_data.py:284-289` shows
("Talmud -- Commentaries").

Fix by assembling the heading from `$a` plus subdivisions and deduping
on a normalized key, in `sources/marc.py`. `_attach_from_candidate` is
the single writer for all three ingest paths, so one fix covers
everything. Deduping in the template would hide the symptom and keep
storing the wrong subject.

Existing tests stay green (`tests/test_marc.py:282-284` covers 650s that
carry only `$a`). Add a case with a subdivided 650 plus a duplicate FAST
650, and an e2e assertion that the confirm page lists each subject once.

The 8 existing Subject rows were written under the truncating logic; a
backfill would need the original MARC, and no stored record has
`source_marc` populated yet.
close_reason: Merged in PR #18

title: Hard-wrap the user-facing docs at 79 columns
description:
`docs/administration.md`, `docs/development.md` and `docs/user-guide.md` are written with unwrapped paragraphs — 52, 59 and 39 lines over 79 columns respectively, some past 500 characters.

CLAUDE.md now distinguishes the two cases: text submitted through GitHub stays unwrapped, because a manual wrap there is lost and produces noisy diffs; Markdown files in the repository are hard-wrapped at 79 columns, because they are read in a terminal as often as in a browser and nothing there reflows a 500-character line. These three files predate that rule and do not follow it.

## Scope

The three files above only. `docs/plans/` is excluded — those are working documents rather than user-facing, and bd-1yg covers what happens to them.

## Do it when the queue is clear

This is a whitespace-only diff across three files, which conflicts with anything else editing them. `docs/administration.md` in particular has been touched by two separate pull requests today. Wait until nothing is open against these files rather than forcing a rebase onto whoever is mid-flight.

Reflow only. No rewording, no restructuring, no corrections — a whitespace commit that also changes prose is unreviewable, because the reviewer cannot tell which is which. Anything worth fixing in the content gets its own change.

Leave fenced code blocks, table rows and long URLs alone; none of those are broken to fit.

Worth checking afterwards whether the pre-commit hook or the process-label lint should enforce the column limit on `docs/*.md`, so this does not drift back. That is a judgement call, not a requirement of this ticket — a hard gate on prose width can be more annoying than the drift it prevents.
close_reason: done

title: Decide whether discarded scans expire on their own
description:
`docs/user-guide.md` tells the reader that discarded scans "are cleaned up automatically after 30 days". Nothing runs automatically. `cleanup_staging` is a management command with a `just cleanup-staging` recipe, and `docs/administration.md` describes it correctly, as something an administrator runs periodically.

Both statements cannot be true, and the false one is the user-facing one. Someone photographing a shelf is being told their discarded images go away on a schedule that does not exist.

This is a product decision before it is a documentation fix. Either the app takes responsibility for expiry, through a scheduled job or an opportunistic sweep on a path that is already cheap, and the user guide becomes true; or it does not, and the user guide says the administrator decides when discarded scans are removed.

Worth deciding deliberately rather than inheriting from whichever document was written last. The images are photographs taken inside someone's home, shop or synagogue, and how long they sit on disk is the kind of thing a user is entitled to a straight answer about.

Whichever way it goes, the two documents have to agree afterward, and `just cleanup-staging [days]` in `docs/development.md` should describe the same behaviour.
close_reason: done

title: Lint the GitHub Actions workflow with zizmor
description:
Nothing checks `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. It is the one file in the tree that runs with a token, and the only review it gets is the same read every other file gets.

`zizmor` is a static analyser for GitHub Actions workflows. Add it to the dev dependencies, run it in `./scripts/check.sh` beside the ruff and process-label checks, and add it to the `lint` job so a workflow change cannot land without it.

## What it finds, measured

Running `zizmor` against `.github/workflows/ci.yml` reports 20 findings, four suppressed: **9 `unpinned-uses`**, **4 `excessive-permissions`**, **3 `artipacked`**, and nothing else. The categories below are those findings rather than a prediction of them.

`.github/workflows/docs.yml` was written against this list and reports only `unpinned-uses`, which is the one deliberately left for the Dependabot work to make maintainable.

## What it will find here

**No `permissions:` block, anywhere.** Not at workflow level, not on any job. Every job therefore runs with whatever the repository default grants, which is more than a test run needs. `permissions: contents: read` at the top, with anything narrower raised per job, is the fix and is the finding most worth having.

**Actions pinned by tag.** `actions/checkout@v4`, `actions/cache@v4`, `astral-sh/setup-uv@v4`. A tag is mutable, so pinning by tag trusts whoever can move it. Pinning by commit SHA with the version in a trailing comment is the answer, and it makes Dependabot's `github-actions` updates more valuable rather than less — Dependabot rewrites the SHA and the comment together.

**Credentials left in the checkout.** `actions/checkout` writes the token into `.git/config` by default and leaves it there for the rest of the job. `persist-credentials: false` on checkouts that do not push is the fix.

The workflow already avoids the sharpest failure: `${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}` reaches the shell through an `env:` binding rather than being interpolated into the `run:` body, which is the correct pattern. The trigger is `pull_request` and not `pull_request_target`. Neither of those is an accident worth undoing.

## Shape

Run it through `uvx` or as a dev dependency — either keeps the version in `uv.lock` and therefore inside the Dependabot cooldown, which is the point of having one.

Findings that are deliberate get an inline suppression carrying the reason, in the same spirit as `# process-label-ok`. A suppression without a reason is a finding that was turned off rather than answered.

Decide the audit level when the first run is in front of you. The default set is the argument for adding it; the pedantic set is worth reading once and then choosing from, rather than adopting wholesale on the strength of it being stricter.

## Verification

`./scripts/check.sh` fails on a workflow with an obvious defect — a job granted `contents: write` it does not need is the easiest one to introduce and revert — and passes on the workflow as fixed. The `lint` job reports the same result CI-side.
close_reason: done

title: pytest-socket is installed but never activated
description:
`pytest-socket` is a declared dev dependency and does nothing. There is no `--disable-socket` in `addopts`, no `disable_socket()` in any conftest, and nothing else turns it on. Tests can open sockets freely.

Verified rather than inferred: a probe test that connects a TCP socket to a public address succeeds during a normal `pytest` run.

## Why it matters

The suite talks to three kinds of remote service in the code it exercises — the Anthropic API for OCR, the SRU catalogs at NLI, LC and DNB, and Open Library for covers. Every test of those paths mocks the client, so nothing reaches the network today. That holds by convention, not by enforcement: a test that forgets a patch, or patches the wrong name, makes a real call and passes.

The Anthropic case is the expensive one — a real vision call costs money per test run and would not obviously look wrong in CI. The catalog case is the rude one: the SRU clients sleep `SRU_REQUEST_DELAY` between requests precisely because these are other people's servers.

This also contradicts what the project has been telling itself. `docs/plans/long-term-plan.md` lists "pytest-socket blocks accidental live HTTP in tests" among the project's strengths, and it has never been true.

## Shape

Enable it, then find out what breaks. `addopts = ["--disable-socket"]` with `--allow-unix-socket` is the usual shape, since the database and the live-server fixture need local sockets.

Expect the e2e suite to need thought rather than a flag. Playwright drives a browser in a separate process, so `pytest-socket` does not constrain it either way — that is a separate hole, and `tests/e2e/test_asset_delivery.py` shows the pattern that does work: a fixture that aborts off-origin requests through the browser context and asserts none were attempted.

Where a test genuinely needs a socket, `@pytest.mark.enable_socket` marks it deliberately, which is the point: the exceptions become visible.
close_reason: done

title: Harvest MARC by role, and use it across lookup, indexing and display
description:
`parse_record` reads a fixed allowlist of fifteen tags: 008, 010, 020, 035, 050, 082, 100, 245, 260, 264, 490, 650, 700, 830, 880. Everything else in a record is discarded at extraction.

Cataloguing practice varies by institution and by era — pre-AACR2, AACR2 and RDA all describe the same book differently, and NLI, LC and DNB each have house habits on top of that. An allowlist encodes one reading of that variation, so every unfamiliar practice is a silent loss and a code change to fix.

The thing that makes a better approach possible: `source_marc` now stores the complete record verbatim on everything created since that landed. Nothing arriving from a catalog is lost, and a richer harvest can be re-derived over stored records later without re-fetching.

## Harvest by role, not by tag

MARC's field groups are semantically consistent even where local practice is not. Collect by what a subfield *is* rather than which tag this cataloguer used:

- **Titles** — 24X, 7XX`$t`, 730, 740, 505`$t`, 4XX and 8XX `$a`
- **Names** — 1XX, 7XX, and the 245`$c` transcription
- **Part designations** — `$n`, `$p`, `$v` wherever they appear: 245, 490, 800, 810, 811, 830
- **Dates** — 008 positions, 260`$c`, 264`$c`, and any four-digit or gematria year in the record

## Three surfaces, three appetites

The harvest is one thing; what each consumer takes from it differs, and conflating them is how this goes wrong.

**External catalog lookup** — query construction and candidate scoring. Maximise recall. A score is a ranking signal rather than a filter, so extra title forms cost a little precision and buy a lot of matching. This is where the harvest should be used most aggressively.

**Internal indexing** — the FTS table. More than today, but not everything: a contents note and added title entries are genuinely useful to a searcher, raw control data is not. Index size and precision are real costs here in a way they are not for scoring.

**Display** — the record page. Canonical fields only, as now. A reader wants one title. A contents note may deserve its own section, but the harvest must not leak into the bibliographic description.

## Caveats to carry into the children

A set record's 505 can list hundreds of volume titles, so whole-note token overlap would score that record highly for any volume of the set. Per-`$t` matching or a low weight, not the raw note.

**No current test fixture contains 246, 505, 730, 740, 800, 810 or 811.** This cannot be built against what is on hand; gathering real multipart-monograph and monographic-series responses is the first child, not an afterthought.

The eleven existing records have no `source_marc` and never will, so a re-derivation pass improves everything created from here on and nothing before it.

title: Gather MARC fixtures for multipart monographs and monographic series
description:
No fixture in `tests/` contains 246, 505, 730, 740, 800, 810 or 811. The harvest work cannot be written against what is on hand, and inventing MARC by hand would encode assumptions about practice rather than testing against it.

Fetch real SRU responses and commit them as fixtures. What is needed, at minimum:

A multipart monograph with a 505 contents note listing volume titles, in both the basic form (one `$a` blob) and the enhanced form (per-volume `$t`/`$r`), since they parse differently and both are in the wild.

A monographic series record carrying 830 with `$n` and `$p`, not only `$a` and `$v`.

A record with 730 or 740 analytic added entries naming individual works.

A record with 246 varying form of title.

A Hebrew record where the alternate script sits in 880s linked to several of the above, since that is the pattern this catalog meets most and the linkage is what makes it hard.

Pull from NLI and LC both — the point of this ticket is capturing how practice differs between them, and a fixture set from one institution would defeat it. DNB too if it has an example worth keeping.

Record in each fixture's filename or a short note what it was chosen to demonstrate, so a later reader knows why it is there and does not delete it as redundant.

title: Harvest titles, names, parts and dates by role from the stored MARC
description:
Build the harvest described in the parent epic: a function over a MARC record that returns every title-bearing string, every name-bearing string, every part designation and every date, gathered by role across field groups rather than from an allowlist of tags.

Keep it separate from `parse_record`. That function produces the canonical values a `Record` is built from and should stay narrow and opinionated — one title, one date, one publisher. The harvest is a second, wider read of the same record for consumers that want recall.

It should work from a stored `source_marc` as readily as from a freshly parsed record, because re-deriving over existing records is what makes the approach durable when the rules improve.

Depends on the fixture-gathering child; there is nothing honest to test against until that lands.

Note that `_subfield_values` in `sources/marc.py` is the single place data-field text is pulled and it strips C1 control characters — the non-sorting delimiters DNB embeds. The harvest must go through it rather than around it.
