title: Use the harvested forms when scoring catalog candidates
description:
`_title_forms` in `sources/score.py` compares three strings: `title`, `title_alternate`, and `volume_part_title` from 245`$p`. A photographed volume of a set therefore fails to match a set record whose volume names live in a 505 note, a 730 analytic entry, or 830`$n`/`$p`.

Feed the harvest into scoring, on the external-lookup side where recall matters most. A score ranks rather than filters, so additional title forms cost a little precision and buy considerable matching.

Two things to get right:

A set record's 505 can list hundreds of volumes. Token overlap against the whole note would score that record highly for any volume of the set, which is worse than not matching at all because it looks like a confident answer. Match per `$t` in the enhanced form, or weight the note well below a title proper.

The score is displayed with per-field verdicts. Decide what a match against a contents note or an analytic entry says to the reader — "title" is misleading when the agreement came from a volume listed in a set record, and the distinction is exactly what the cataloguer needs to judge the row.

Depends on the harvest child.

comments.author: dchud
comments.text: Good candidate for a stronger reasoning model (fable). The work is judgement over ambiguous material rather than implementation: getting it wrong produces something plausible that is quietly incorrect, which review does not reliably catch. Those sessions are expensive, so space them out rather than running several at once.

title: Decide what the harvest adds to the local search index
description:
The FTS index covers title, romanized title, subtitle, authors, subjects, publishers, place, notes, identifiers, provenance and the ownership marks, plus a Hebrew stems column. The harvest offers more: contents notes, analytic added entries, varying titles, series part names.

This is a different judgement from candidate scoring. Scoring ranks a handful of rows and tolerates noise; the index answers a user's query and pays for every extra token in size and in precision. Somebody searching for a volume title probably does want to find the set record that contains it — but a contents note listing two hundred volumes makes that record match two hundred queries.

Decide per source what earns indexing, and where it goes. `FTS_TEXT_COLUMNS` maps a column to a `Record` attribute, so anything indexed has to be stored on the record — which means deciding what the harvest contributes to the model, not only to the index. A separate weighted column, as the Hebrew stems work did, is one shape worth considering.

The record page is the third consumer and wants least: canonical fields, with a contents note plausibly earning its own section. The harvest must not leak into the bibliographic description.

Depends on the harvest child, and is worth doing after the scoring child so there is evidence about which sources actually carry useful text.

comments.author: dchud
comments.text: Good candidate for a stronger reasoning model (fable). The work is judgement over ambiguous material rather than implementation: getting it wrong produces something plausible that is quietly incorrect, which review does not reliably catch. Those sessions are expensive, so space them out rather than running several at once.

title: Show the queue on /ingest/ and its depth in the ingest mode bar
description:
`/ingest/` renders three cards -- Scan barcode, Photograph title page,
Enter manually -- that the ingest mode bar (commit 25f39b3) now carries
on every ingest page. The cards duplicate the bar directly above them,
and the only thing left that is unique to the page is a "Review queue"
link.

Two changes, one dependent on the other:

`/ingest/` renders the queue itself. The route choice is already in the
bar, so the landing page can show what is waiting rather than repeating
the navigation. `/ingest/queue/` keeps working and renders the same
view.

The mode bar gains a Queue item carrying the pending count. This is the
part that answers "did what I just scanned land?" -- right after a scan
the user is standing on `/ingest/scan/`, not on the landing page, so a
count that lives only on `/ingest/` still has to be gone looking for.
The count is per-user, matching the existing queue scoping (staff see
all).

Depends on bd-queue-rows-r91 for what the rows look like; this ticket is
about where the queue appears and how its depth is surfaced.

## Testing

E2e that `/ingest/` lists pending scans, that the bar shows a count that
tracks what is actually pending, and that the count is visible at phone
width.

title: Rework the interface as a designed system rather than a prototype
description:
What exists today is an early functional prototype. It works, it is tested, and it was built one ticket at a time — which was the right way to get here and is why it looks like it. Roughly twenty screens accreted independently: nine browse views, search, record detail, three ingest paths, the review queue, confirm, phone capture.

There is no design system. No documented type scale, no spacing rhythm, no colour roles, no component inventory. Tailwind utilities are chosen per template, which is why a shared candidate row had to be extracted by hand the first time two screens needed one.

The goal is an interface that shows dense bibliographic information clearly, with navigation a person can hold in their head. That is a different activity from the ticket-per-feature rhythm that built the prototype, and it should not start until the functionality underneath it has settled.

## When to start

Deliberately not now. Designing against functionality that is still moving means doing it twice. The backlog still has ingest, series, harvest and authority work that changes what the screens must show.

Reasonable entry conditions, to be judged rather than counted: the ingest paths stable enough that no screen is about to gain or lose a step; the candidate and queue surfaces settled after the scoring and harvest work; enough records loaded that density problems are visible, since they do not appear on eleven.

## The shape of the work, in outline

Detail is deliberately deferred to children filed when this starts. The intended sequence:

Inventory every screen as it actually renders, at phone and desktop widths, with real records — not from reading templates, which has proved unreliable.

Establish what each screen is *for*: the decision a person makes there, and what information serves it. The candidate list is the sharp case, where the whole ingest workflow narrows to "is this my book?".

Then the problems specific to this catalog, which generic interface advice does not address: bidirectional text sharing a line, a cell and a title; density against scannability in MARC-derived data; two devices showing one scan at once; and conveying match confidence without inviting people to accept it blindly.

Then a small written system — type scale, spacing, colour roles including direction-aware ones, a component inventory — so the next feature does not re-invent a card.

Then screen by screen, each its own change with end-to-end coverage.

## The part not to defer

See the child ticket on end-to-end locators. Around half of the current locators bind to CSS classes and element ids, which a redesign breaks. Every browser test written between now and then adds to that bill, and the fix costs nothing if applied as tests are written.

title: Prefer semantic locators in end-to-end tests
description:
About half the locators in `tests/e2e/` bind to markup rather than meaning: `.btn-busy`, `.btn-idle`, `#capture-error`, `[id^='title-page-card-']`. Roughly 29 such locators against 28 semantic ones, across 22 files.

A markup-coupled locator asserts that a particular class or id exists, which is a fact about the current templates rather than about what a user can do. Rename the class and the test fails though nothing a person experiences has changed; keep the class while breaking the behaviour and the test passes. The interface rework will rename a great many of them.

Semantic locators — `get_by_role`, `get_by_label`, `get_by_text` — survive a redesign, and they fail for the right reason, because they describe the thing the user is looking for.

## Two halves, and only one is urgent

**Going forward, as a convention.** New browser tests should prefer semantic locators, falling back to a `data-testid` where a control genuinely has no accessible name — which is itself a signal worth noticing, since a control a test cannot name by role or label is usually one a screen reader cannot either. This costs nothing when applied as tests are written, and every test written without it adds to the eventual bill. Worth writing into CLAUDE.md alongside the existing rule that user-visible changes need a browser test.

**The existing 29, retrospectively.** Lower value and can wait for the rework, which will touch those tests anyway. Converting them now means editing tests without changing behaviour, which is hard to review and easy to get subtly wrong.

Do the convention. Leave the backlog of existing locators to the rework unless one is already in a file being changed for another reason.
close_reason: done

title: Strip volume qualifiers out of ISBNs and keep what they say
description:
`parse_record` reads `result["isbn"] = get_field_value(marc_record, "020", ["a"])`, which is correct against the format and wrong against what NLI sends.

The same book, catalogued by both endpoints, stored as fixtures in `tests/fixtures/marc/`:

```
LC    020 $a 9780827609426  $q v. 1
NLI   020 $a 9780827609426 (v. [1])
```

`$q` is the qualifier subfield and LC uses it. NLI writes the qualifier into `$a` alongside the number. Reading `$a` therefore yields an ISBN from one catalog and a string that is not an ISBN from the other, for the same book.

Two consequences, both visible in the catalog already. `otzar-9` carries `ISBN=9780827609426 (v. [1])` in `ExternalIdentifier.value` while `otzar-a` — the same work from LC — carries `9780827609426`. They do not match, so the two records do not deduplicate, an ISBN lookup for that book finds one of them, and the identifier stored is not one anybody can look up anywhere else.

## What to do

Take the digits and the check character, and nothing else, for the value that goes in `ExternalIdentifier`. An ISBN is a fixed shape and the trailing parenthetical is not part of it.

Keep what was stripped rather than discarding it. `(v. [1])` and `$q v. 1` are the same statement in two places, and both say which volume this ISBN belongs to — a set-membership signal that neither reading currently uses. Store it where the volume work can find it rather than making that work re-parse the field later.

`020 $z` holds a cancelled or invalid ISBN and NLI sends those too, in the same record and with the same qualifier habit. A `$z` value should not become an identifier anybody can match on, and should not be silently dropped either.

## One record, many ISBNs

The NLI record for this work carries six `020` fields, one per volume of the set. That is the case where a single bibliographic record stands for the whole set and the enumeration lives nowhere else. Whatever reads 020 has to expect a list rather than a value, and the first one is not more authoritative than the rest.

## Tests

An NLI-style `020 $a` with an inline qualifier yields a bare ISBN and a preserved volume designation. An LC-style `$a` plus `$q` yields the same pair. A record carrying both forms across several 020 fields yields one entry per volume. A `$z` value does not become a matchable identifier. Two records for one book, one from each catalog, produce the same ISBN.
close_reason: done

title: Repair the corrupted title on the existing DNB record
description:
Record `otzar-e` has the title `\x98The\x9c Complete Piano Etudes`. U+0098 and U+009C are the MARC non-sorting delimiters DNB wraps around a leading article, and browsers render them as blank, so the title reads as though it has stray whitespace in it.

Stripping them at parse time stops new records carrying them, but does nothing for rows already written. This is the data repair for what is already stored.

Depends on bd-osc landing first, so the parser and the repair agree on what a clean value looks like.

## Shape

A one-off management command, or a data migration if the set is small enough to enumerate. Scan every text field on `Record`, `Author`, `Publisher` and `Subject` for C1 control characters rather than assuming only titles carry them — the delimiters are legal in any MARC field with a non-sorting portion, and only titles have been checked.

Report what was found before changing anything. The live catalog is small enough that the honest first step is counting the affected rows and fields.

The FTS index in `catalog/search.py` holds its own copy of the indexed text, so a repaired record has to be re-indexed or the old bytes stay searchable.
close_reason: Merged in PR #25

title: Search and browse quality: prefix matching, Hebrew prefixes, facets, related items
description:
Catalog search matches whole tokens only, the site navigation links to the search page instead of carrying a search box, results cannot be narrowed, and the record page relates items by author and series but not by subject. Each is a bounded change to `catalog/search.py`, the search views, or the record detail view; none needs a different search engine. FTS5 is adequate at a few thousand records and stays.

Children, in the order they matter: prefix matching, then Hebrew prefix particles, then the navigation search box, then same-subject related items, then facets once the catalog is large enough that narrowing a result list is a real need.

Browse views sort by Unicode code point, not language-aware collation. Hebrew sorts acceptably because of code-point order; Latin titles with diacritics can sort oddly. No ticket for that until a browse page is seen to be wrong.

title: Match word prefixes in catalog search
description:
`_sanitize_query` in `catalog/search.py` quotes every word, so the FTS5 MATCH expression requires whole-token matches: `Rambam` finds records containing that token, `Ramb` finds nothing. Typing part of a name or title is the common case at a search box. The user guide says "Partial words match", which is wrong; its own example is a whole word.

FTS5 supports prefix queries natively: `"ramb"*` matches any token starting with `ramb`. Append `*` to each quoted word, or to the last word only, and check ranking on the test dataset so an exact token still outranks a prefix hit. The table is created with the default tokenizer (`ensure_fts_table`), so confirm how Hebrew tokens with attached geresh, gershayim or maqaf split before relying on prefix semantics for them.

Correct the user guide passage. Unit tests for prefix hits and for exact-over-prefix ranking; e2e for a partial-word search reaching the expected record.
close_reason: Merged in PR #53

title: Strip Hebrew prefix particles at index and query time
description:
A search for ספר does not match a record whose title carries הספר, בספר or לספר. The tokenizer splits on whitespace and punctuation, and the attached prefix letters (ב, ה, ו, כ, ל, מ, ש) are part of the token. A reader searching for a Hebrew word expects the inflected forms to match; the user guide documents this as a known limitation.

Two bounded options, either applied at both index time and query time so they agree. Index each Hebrew token as written and again with plausible leading prefix letters stripped, so a plain query for the base form matches; this keeps the query builder unchanged at the cost of a slightly larger index. Or expand the query to OR the written form with each prefix-stripped form. Indexing the extra forms is simpler to reason about.

Stripping is lossy in both directions, since the first letter of a word can be a real prefix or part of the root. Treat this as recall, not precision: an extra match costs less than a miss. Touches the same function as the prefix-matching ticket; land them in either order.
close_reason: Merged in PR #53

title: Put a search box in the site navigation
description: The header in `templates/base.html` carries a link to `/search/`, so a search starts with a click, a page load, then typing. A search box in the navigation submits straight to the search view from any page. `search_views.py` already reads `q` from GET, so this is a form in the header plus layout at phone width, where the box has to fit beside the existing links or collapse behind the menu. Keep the 44px touch targets and the focus ring styling the header uses. E2e: submit a query from the home page header and land on results.
close_reason: done

title: Show same-subject items on the record page
description:
`record_detail` in `catalog/views.py` relates a record to other works by the same authors and to sibling volumes in its series, and not to records sharing a subject heading. For a collection where subjects are the organizing vocabulary (a tractate, a halakhic topic, commentaries on one book), same-subject items are the most useful related list after series siblings, and they are one query: records sharing any subject with this one, excluding itself, ordered by the number of shared subjects.

Cap the list as the author list is capped and render it under the same heading style. "Shelved nearby" (records at adjacent locations) is a separate idea that needs an ordering over `Location` labels, which are free text; it stays out of scope until locations are assigned consistently enough to sort.
close_reason: done

title: Filter search results by language, decade and location
description:
Search results are one ranked list with no way to narrow them. Facets for language (the stored code, shown through `language_name`), publication decade (from `date_of_publication`), and location map directly onto fields the record carries, and the browse views already group by decade and by location.

Not needed while the catalog holds a few dozen records; a query that returns eight results does not need narrowing. The trigger is a search that regularly returns more than one screen. Implementation: fetch the FTS hit list, then filter the `Record` queryset by the chosen facet values, since FTS5 ranks and the ORM filters; per-value counts come from the filtered queryset.

title: Render language codes as language names
description:
Language shows as the raw code -- `heb` rather than `Hebrew` -- on the
record detail page, the ingest confirm page, the scan poll partial, the
manual entry form, and in the admin filter.

## The trap

MARC 008/35-37 carries ISO 639-2/**B** bibliographic codes, so German is
`ger`, not `deu`. `sources/marc.py:197` reads exactly those bytes, and
`catalog/language_views.py:19` already stores the bibliographic form.

`pycountry` (already a dependency) indexes ISO 639-3, where these exist
only as a `bibliographic` alias:

    pycountry.languages.get(alpha_3="ger")       -> None
    pycountry.languages.get(bibliographic="ger") -> German

An alpha_3-only lookup renders German, French, Dutch, Greek, Czech,
Persian, Chinese, Romanian, Welsh, Basque, Armenian, Icelandic,
Georgian, Macedonian, Maori, Malay, Burmese, Slovak, Albanian and
Tibetan as blank -- 20 divergences. Bibliographic lookup must come
first.

## Shape

A plain module `catalog/language_codes.py` plus a template filter
library, following the existing `bidi` templatetag pattern. Shared
rather than living inside the templatetag because
`catalog/language_views.py` is a second consumer.

Two display sites render plain dicts from session/JSON rather than model
instances, so this has to be a filter, not a model property.

A small override table is needed for MARC codes withdrawn from ISO 639-2
that ISO 639-3 has since reassigned -- `gae` means Scottish Gaelic in a
pre-1997 record, but pycountry answers "Guarequena" -- plus a few codes
whose 639-3 scholarly names read oddly on a catalog page (`arc` ->
Aramaic, not "Official Aramaic (700-300 BCE)").

Do not store the display name at ingest time: the code is the
interchange value, it round-trips against `source_marc`, and a stored
name drifts when a cataloger edits the code.

## Testing

Unit tests covering the B/T divergence specifically (`ger`, `fre`,
`dut`, `gre`, `cze`, `per`), the codes this catalog actually uses
(`heb`, `yid`, `lad`, `jrb`, `jpr`, `sam`), the overrides, case and
whitespace normalization, and passthrough for unknown codes. E2e
assertions on record detail and the confirm page, including a German
record -- that is the case a naive fix renders blank.

Also fix `tests/test_views.py:18`, which sets `language="Hebrew"`, a
display name in a code field.

title: source_marc is never populated on records created from a lookup
description:
`Record.source_marc` is meant to hold the archival MARC the record was built from. It is always null: 0 of 11 records have it populated.

`_create_record_from_candidate` sets `source_marc=candidate.get("source_marc")`, but `parse_record` in `sources/marc.py` never emits that key, so the value is `None` on every record the ISBN and title-page paths create.

The field is dead weight in the schema and in the admin, and anything needing to re-derive a value from the original record has nothing to work from.

## Existing rows cannot be backfilled

The source documents were never kept. Fixing the write path does nothing for the records already in the catalog, and there is no local data to recover them from — the only route would be re-fetching each record from NLI, LC or DNB by identifier, which is a separate piece of work and not always possible.

So `source_marc` will be null for the oldest records permanently. Anything built on the field has to tolerate that rather than assuming presence. Accepted deliberately; the point of the fix is that it stops being true for everything created from here on.

## Shape

Have `parse_record` carry the source record through, or have the callers attach it. Prefer whichever keeps the parsed dict serializable, since `candidate_records` is a JSONField and the candidate dict round-trips through the session on the confirm path.

Storing the record verbatim is the point: it is the archival source document, so it should not be cleaned or normalized on the way in. The extraction path is where cleaning belongs.

Check the size cost before committing to it. A MARC record is a few kilobytes, `candidate_records` holds a list of them per scan, and they travel through the session on the confirm path.

Found while fixing bd-osc and bd-fv6.
close_reason: Merged in PR #24

title: Move author VIAF identifiers into the generalized identifier model
description:
`Author.viaf_id` is a `CharField` on the model, while every other external identifier otzar stores goes through `ExternalIdentifier`. The split exists because `ExternalIdentifier` can only point at a `Record`, and a VIAF ID names an author. `ExternalIdentifier.IDENTIFIER_TYPES` declares a `VIAF` choice that nothing writes — the dead choice is the visible symptom of the workaround.

`bd-tz2s.3` generalizes `ExternalIdentifier` with nullable foreign keys to `record`, `series` and `author` and a constraint that exactly one is set. Once that lands, the author case has a home and the column becomes the one entity whose identifier lives somewhere else.

## What moves

`viaf_id` is read and written across `ingest/authority.py` and `ingest/management/commands/enrich_authors.py`, including `Author.objects.filter(viaf_id="")` to find unenriched authors, a duplicate check on `Author.objects.filter(viaf_id=cluster.viaf_id).exclude(pk=author.pk)`, and a conflict check comparing a stored ID against a freshly found one. Each becomes a query through the related identifier rather than a column lookup, and the "unenriched" query inverts: authors with no VIAF identifier row, rather than authors with an empty string.

The admin exposes `viaf_id` in `list_display`, `search_fields` and `list_filter` on `AuthorAdmin`; those move to the related model. `docs/development.md` describes the column under `Author` and needs to describe the relationship instead.

## Why it is worth doing rather than living with

Two storage shapes for one concept means every future identifier faces the same choice with no principle to settle it, and the answer will keep being decided by which entity happened to need it first. One rule that fits in a sentence — an identifier names exactly one entity — is worth a migration in a project with no installed base.

The counter-argument is that `viaf_id` is queried directly and often, and a column is faster than a join. That is real but small at this collection's size, and an index on the identifier value covers the queries that matter.

## Tests

Enrichment still sets and reads the identifier through the new path; the unenriched-author query finds authors with no VIAF row and skips those that have one; the duplicate check still catches two authors carrying the same VIAF ID; the conflict check still fires when a stored ID disagrees with a found one. A record, a series and an author each carry their own identifier without collision, and the constraint rejects a row that names none or more than one.

title: Fix repository drift: unused pymarc, MkDocs claim, OCR model default in the administration guide
description:
Three small mismatches between what the repository says and what it does.

`pymarc>=5.3.1` is in `pyproject.toml` and nothing imports it; the MARC library in use is `mrrc`. Remove it and update `uv.lock`.

`CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` list Material for MkDocs as the documentation tool and there is no `mkdocs.yml`; `docs/` is plain Markdown. Either add the MkDocs configuration and a `just docs` target, or drop the line from both files. Plain Markdown has served so far; MkDocs is only worth adding if the docs are going to be published.

`docs/administration.md` gives `claude-sonnet-4-6` as the `CLAUDE_MODEL` default. The code default in `ingest/ocr.py`, `.env.example` and `docs/development.md` is `claude-sonnet-5`. Fix the table row. bd-mej rewrites the Fly sections of the same file; do this in whichever lands second.
close_reason: done

title: Strip MARC non-sorting delimiters from imported text
description:
Record `otzar-e` has the title `\x98The\x9c Complete Piano Etudes`.
U+0098 and U+009C are the MARC non-sorting character delimiters, which
DNB wraps around a leading article so it does not affect sort order.
Browsers render them as blank, so the title reads as though it has
stray whitespace in it.

`sources/marc.py:153` takes 245$a+$b through `get_field_value` verbatim,
and nothing downstream removes C1 control characters. Any DNB-sourced
field with a leading article carries them.

Strip the C1 range at parse time so they never reach the database, and
repair the one existing record. Worth checking whether NLI or LC use the
same convention before assuming this is DNB-only.

Found while reviewing a record in the browser during title-page work.

title: Score search candidates against the extracted metadata
description:
Candidates come back ordered by source catalog and by each catalog's own relevance, which has no knowledge of the photographed page. A title-only fallback query returns forty editions of Leviticus in arbitrary order, and the reader has to compare each row against the photo by eye. The OCR output is right there and is never used for anything after the query is built.

Score each candidate against the extracted metadata and order by agreement, across catalogs rather than within them.

## Shape

A pure function in `sources/` — `score_candidate(metadata, record)` returning a score and a per-field verdict list — so it is testable without network access and usable from both the cascade view and any later batch tooling. The view sorts by score before rendering; nothing else about the search path changes.

Score over the fields present on both sides, so a sparse catalog record is not punished for what it omits, with a small tiebreaker for the number of fields that agreed. Suggested weights: title heaviest, then author, date, publisher, place. Keep the result in 0..1 so it can be displayed.

Token-set overlap on normalized tokens suits this better than character-ratio fuzzy matching, given Hebrew and romanized forms sitting side by side. `difflib` is enough; no new dependency.

## Per-field normalization

Each field needs its own comparison, and these are the cases this catalog actually produces:

Title — strip MARC display punctuation (` /`, ` :`, ` =`), compare the Hebrew title against the record's title and its 880 alternate, and separately compare the romanized title. Normalize gershayim and geresh against ASCII quotes and apostrophes, strip niqqud.

Author — catalog form is inverted ("Herczeg, Yisrael Isser Zvi"), OCR form is not. Compare as token sets, and check the record's additional authors, not only the first.

Publisher — the same corporate-suffix normalizer that the query builder needs. Build it once and use it in both places.

Place — "Brooklyn, N.Y." against "Brooklyn, New York", plus trailing MARC punctuation.

Date — extract four-digit years from both sides and allow a near miss; catalog dates arrive as `[1999]`, `c1999`, `1994-2003`. A Hebrew year on the title page has no Gregorian form to compare against unless the OCR prompt is asked for both, which is worth doing while the prompt is being reworked for schema-constrained output.

## What the reader sees

The score matters less than the reason for it. Show which fields agreed on each row — title and publisher matched, date did not — so the ordering explains itself and a wrong match is visible rather than hidden behind a number. Never auto-select; the list stays as evidence.

A top score that is very low is also a signal that the query fell through to a broad step, and pairs with surfacing the matched cascade step.

## Testing

Fixtures from real pairs, including a set record matched against a photographed volume, a Hebrew title carrying gershayim, and a record whose only agreement is the publisher.
close_reason: Merged in PR #52

title: Remove the Fly.io deployment
description:
The app has never been deployed to Fly.io and will not be. The deploy workflow runs on every push to `main` and fails every time, so every merge carries a red X that means nothing.

## Remove

`.github/workflows/deploy.yml` — the whole `deploy` job. Note the `test` job in that file duplicates what `ci.yml` already runs, so the file goes entirely rather than being trimmed.

`fly.toml` — machine size, volume mount, health check and autostop, none of which apply anywhere else.

Fly-specific prose in `docs/deployment.md` and `docs/administration.md`. Both are written around flyctl commands and a Fly volume at `/data`, so this is a rewrite rather than an edit; bd-n7a is what replaces them. Leaving stale instructions for a platform we do not use is worse than having none.

The Fly comments in `.env.example` (lines 12, 17, 33-34) and the `/data` comment in `otzar/settings.py:71`. `DATA_DIR` itself stays — it is a sound abstraction and the next platform needs it too.

## Keep

`Dockerfile` and `entrypoint.sh` carry no Fly coupling. They build a container that migrates and starts gunicorn, which is what any container platform wants. The `FLY_API_TOKEN` secret in the GitHub repo settings can be revoked once the workflow is gone; that is a manual step in the web UI.

`docs/plans/` also mentions Fly, and is exempt from this: those are planning documents that record what was true when written, and bd-1yg covers retiring them.

## Check before closing

`/health/` exists for the Fly health check. Keep it — any platform wants one — but confirm nothing else referenced the endpoint only for Fly's benefit.

Ordering: this can land before bd-n7a decides anything. Removing a workflow that only ever fails does not depend on knowing what replaces it.
close_reason: Merged in PR #26

title: Record author roles from MARC relator terms and codes
description:
The record-to-author link holds only a record id and an author id, so a translator, an editor and the author of the original text all attach to a record identically. The catalog page lists them side by side as if all stood in the same relation to the book.

This is the half of otzar-55i that was not built. The other half — transcribing 245`$c`, the statement of responsibility — landed already, and it covers the common case in prose: "translated, annotated, and elucidated by Yisrael Isser Zvi Herczeg ; in collaboration with Yaakov Petroff". That answers "who did what" for a reader. It does not give the catalog structured roles it can browse or filter on.

## What the data actually supports

MARC carries roles in `700$e` (relator term, e.g. "translator") and `700$4` (relator code, e.g. `trl`), both optional and both frequently absent. The LC record in otzar-55i has four `700` fields and neither subfield on any of them, which is why the roles exist only in the `$c` prose there. NLI records carry relators more often.

So the ceiling on this work is what the catalogs supply. Build it for the records that have relators, leave the rest unroled, and do not attempt to parse roles out of `$c` prose — otzar-55i rules that out explicitly and it is a trap: the prose is free text in two scripts with no controlled vocabulary behind it.

## Shape

A role field on the through table between `Record` and `Author`, which means an explicit `through` model and a migration. `Record.authors` is currently a plain `ManyToManyField`, so this is a schema change with a data migration for existing links, not an added column.

`sources/marc.py` reads `700` fields in `_attach_from_candidate`'s input today and keeps only the name. It needs to carry the relator term and code alongside each additional author.

The `$4` codes are from the MARC Relator Code list and need mapping to display terms. Prefer the code where both are present — `$e` is free text and varies in capitalisation and punctuation between catalogs.

Decide what an unroled author displays as. "Author" is a guess and will sometimes be wrong; showing nothing is honest but makes the roled and unroled cases look inconsistent on the same page.

## Sequencing

Touches `catalog/models.py` and a migration, `sources/marc.py`, `ingest/views.py` and the record detail page — four files that other work contends for. Worth picking up when those are quiet rather than forcing it alongside them.
delete_reason: duplicate; the create succeeded while its export failed, so the retry made a second

title: Plan an AWS deployment with S3 backups and a tested restore
description:
Replace the abandoned Fly.io target with an AWS deployment: a deploy that is one command, backups that happen without being remembered, and a restore that has been run rather than described. This ticket is the planning work. What follows is a recommendation for the owner to ratify, with the alternatives costed so a different choice can be made on the same grounds. Implementation is in the child tickets listed at the end; they are written so that only the provisioning ticket changes if the platform does.

## The constraint

The database is one SQLite file at `DATA_DIR/db.sqlite3` in WAL mode (`otzar/settings.py`), and search is an FTS5 virtual table, `catalog_fts`, in the same file (`catalog/search.py`). The index is derived data, rebuilt by `reindex_all()`, but it travels with the file: any file-level copy carries it. One writer, on a local disk, in one process. That rules out anything that treats the filesystem as ephemeral (App Runner, Lightsail's container service), anything that runs more than one instance, and network filesystems: SQLite's own documentation says NFS locking is unreliable, EFS users report stale locks and corruption under concurrent access, every lock and fsync becomes a network round trip, and Litestream also wants a local file. Fargate with EFS is therefore ruled out on evidence, not preference. What remains is one small always-on machine with a disk that persists, which is what the container was written for.

## Recommendation

Lightsail, the 1 GB / 2 vCPU / 40 GB dual-stack Linux bundle, Ubuntu 24.04, Docker and Caddy on the instance, in us-east-1. Two S3 buckets in the same region: media (versioned, served through presigned URLs) and backups (Litestream replica plus dated snapshots). Media goes to S3 through Django's storage API. CI builds the image for every commit on `main` and pushes it to GHCR; the owner deploys a chosen image with `just deploy`, which restarts the container over SSH. Restore is rehearsed on a throwaway instance and the result written down. About $8 to $9 a month.

## Compute, costed

On-demand list prices, us-east-1, September 2026.

- Lightsail 1 GB bundle: $7/month, includes 2 vCPU, 40 GB SSD, 2 TB transfer, a static IPv4 and the firewall. Automatic daily snapshots (seven kept) at $0.05 per GB-month, roughly $0.50 at this disk's fill. The 2 GB bundle is $12.
- EC2 t4g.micro (1 GB, Graviton): $6.13/month, plus gp3 20 GB $1.60, plus the public IPv4 charge $3.65, plus EBS snapshots about $0.50: about $12. t4g.small (2 GB): about $18. A one-year savings plan takes roughly a third off the instance line; not worth committing to before the first deploy.
- Fargate 0.25 vCPU / 0.5 GB: about $9/month for the task, plus IPv4 $3.65, plus EFS, plus either an ALB (about $16) or a task IP that changes on every deploy. Ruled out above on SQLite grounds regardless of price.
- App Runner: no persistent disk. Ruled out unless the database leaves SQLite, which is out of scope.
- Common to every option: S3 under $1/month at this catalog's size (storage $0.023/GB-month; Litestream's request volume at the 1 s sync interval is a few thousand PUTs a month of light cataloging at $0.005 per thousand); GHCR and Actions free on a public repository; DNS free at the registrar or $0.50 for a Route 53 zone; Caddy and Let's Encrypt free. The free tier is not planned around: accounts created since July 2025 get credits rather than free instance hours, and Lightsail's three-month trial applies to the paid plan only.

What drives the cost is the always-on instance, which the single-writer design requires, and the IPv4 address (bundled in Lightsail, $3.65 on EC2). Storage and S3 do not register.

Why Lightsail over EC2: it is $4 to $6 a month cheaper for the same memory once IPv4 and the disk are counted; there is nothing to design (no VPC, security group, EBS volume, AMI or role: the bundle is machine, disk, IP, firewall and snapshots); it is the closest analogue to the Fly machine and volume the container was written against; and Lightsail can export an instance to EC2 if the needs grow. What EC2 would buy, for the owner to weigh: an instance role, so no static access key sits on the box (Lightsail cannot attach one, so Litestream and the media backend authenticate with a key for an IAM user scoped to the two buckets, kept in the instance's `.env`, rotated by hand); Graviton, which is cheaper per unit of work but irrelevant at this load; resizing in place with a stop and start, where Lightsail needs a snapshot and a relaunch; and CloudWatch integration. If the owner values the instance role more than $5 a month and a shorter provisioning script, choose t4g.micro; only the provisioning ticket changes.

Memory: 1 GB is enough. OS and Docker about 250 MB, Caddy 30 MB, two gunicorn workers about 250 MB, Litestream 30 MB; image builds happen in CI, not on the box; the browser resizes photos to 1500 px before upload so Pillow's peak is small. Add a 1 GB swap file. If `free -m` shows swap in steady use, snapshot and relaunch on the 2 GB bundle.

## Media

`media/` holds staged title-page photos and, after bd-yg9, the photos attached to records: large, append-mostly, no transactional consistency needed. Two workable answers. On the instance disk, served by Caddy, synced hourly to a versioned bucket: no new dependency, dev and production identical, but the disk becomes a second system of record, restore has a second step, and the machine is stateful in two places. On S3 through `django-storages`, switched on by an environment variable: the machine then holds only the database, which Litestream already streams, so machine loss costs nothing in media and the restore is one mechanism; bucket versioning is the media backup; the disk never fills. The costs are a dependency (`django-storages` and `boto3`), a code path CI does not run (covered by a post-deploy smoke test that uploads a photo), and on Lightsail the static key. The code already goes through the storage API everywhere (`scan.image.open`, `scan.image.delete`, `.url`; nothing reads `.path`), so the change is settings, not application code. Recommendation: S3. Whichever is chosen, it has to be chosen before the first deploy: `otzar/urls.py` serves `/media/` only when `DEBUG` is true, so production today serves no images at all.

## Backups

Two mechanisms, because they protect against different things.

Continuous replication, Litestream in the container image, replica at `s3://<backup bucket>/litestream/db`, sync interval 1 s, snapshot every 24 h, retention 168 h. Losing the machine loses at most the last second of writes, and any moment in the last seven days is restorable with `-timestamp`. The default retention of 24 h is too short to be useful for a mistake noticed the next day, so it is raised.

Dated snapshots, a management command run daily by a host timer and by the deploy script before every deploy: `sqlite3.Connection.backup()` (the online-backup API, safe against a live WAL database) to a temporary file, gzipped, uploaded to `snapshots/YYYY/MM/DD/` with a manifest holding the record count and the commit; copied to `monthly/` on the first of the month. Lifecycle rules expire `snapshots/` after 35 days and `monthly/` after 400. These are self-contained SQLite files anyone can download and open with `sqlite3`, with no dependence on Litestream's format or on knowing when the damage happened. A bad migration or a mistaken bulk edit is undone from the pre-deploy snapshot or from the day before.

What retention buys is the maximum delay between a mistake and noticing it: seven days to the second, 35 days to the day, 13 months to the month. The whole of it costs cents.

Media: bucket versioning with noncurrent versions expiring after 30 days. Instance snapshots (daily, seven kept) roll back the machine itself, not the catalog. Not backed up, deliberately: `DATA_DIR/cache` (derived) and `staticfiles` (in the image).

## Restore

Executed on a throwaway instance launched by the same provisioning script, with replication switched off and a read-only IAM key so the drill cannot write into the production replica or the media bucket. Both paths are run: `litestream restore` (latest and `-timestamp`) and a snapshot file gunzipped into place. Verification, each value recorded: `Record.objects.count()` equals the manifest's or production's count read before the restore; one record chosen at drill time has the same title, authors and identifiers; a search on a word from that title returns it, with `manage.py reindex` run and noted if it does not, since the FTS table and its shadow tables are in the same file and should not need it; the record's image returns 200; `/health/` returns 200 through Caddy. The date, commit, snapshot, counts and outcome are written into `docs/administration.md`, and the drill is repeated after any change to the backup path and otherwise quarterly.

## Deploy

One command. After every required check passes on a commit to `main`, a CI job builds the image (`linux/amd64` for Lightsail; `linux/arm64` on GitHub's free ARM runner if the host is Graviton) and pushes `ghcr.io/dchud/otzar:<sha>`. The owner runs `just deploy [sha]`, which refuses a SHA that is not on `main` or has no published image, then SSHes to the instance as the owner and runs `deploy.sh`: pre-deploy snapshot, `docker compose pull`, `docker compose up -d`, wait for `/health/`, print backup freshness. Migrations run automatically in the entrypoint as they do today; the pre-deploy snapshot is the rollback point. Secrets: the instance's `/opt/otzar/.env` (root, 0600) holds every application secret and the bucket key, written by hand once; GitHub holds nothing for the instance, since the image job needs only `GITHUB_TOKEN` and deploys run from the owner's machine; bd-n7a.5 records why this was chosen over deploying on every merge. Parameter Store with an instance role is the EC2 variant; Secrets Manager's per-secret charge buys nothing here. The entrypoint refuses to start when `DATA_DIR` is unset or is `/app`, because an unset `DATA_DIR` silently runs against the image's own filesystem and the next deploy discards the catalog.

## Public exposure

The site is a private catalog with no public audience, on one small burstable instance. What gives out first under unwanted traffic is CPU, and the most expensive thing a stranger can ask for is a password check: each login attempt costs a PBKDF2 hash, and django-axes, which locks a username at an address, does not stop a run that rotates either. The posture:

- The site password gate stands in front of the login pages, so only someone holding the shared password can reach a hash (bd-aau2). `SITE_PASSWORD` is required in production.
- Crawlers are told to stay out with `robots.txt` and `X-Robots-Tag` (bd-se7v).
- Caddy caps request bodies at 15 MB (bd-n7a.4).
- A burst-capacity alarm reports sustained load (bd-n7a.4).
- Two switches are ready: a maintenance page in Caddy and a firewall allowlist in Lightsail (bd-n7a.5).

Considered and left out for now, each with a known path back in:

- Cloudflare in front. It would add DDoS absorption, crawler blocking and an "under attack" mode, but moves the DNS for all of `onebiglibrary.net`, and `otzar/client_ip.py` would have to read `CF-Connecting-IP` instead of the last `X-Forwarded-For` entry, or axes would lock out Cloudflare's edge addresses. The owner declined it.
- CloudFront, and AWS WAF with it. Nothing here is cacheable (every page is gated or personal), so CloudFront alone does not reduce the load that matters; the rate-based rules are WAF's, at roughly $7 to $10 a month, about the cost of the instance. It would also need an ACM certificate, a secret-header check in Caddy so the origin cannot be reached around it, and the client-address change above.
- Per-address rate limiting at the origin, through the `caddy-ratelimit` plugin (a custom Caddy build) or fail2ban on Caddy's access log. Worth adding if the load alarm fires with the gate in place.

## Out of scope

Moving off SQLite: a large change with its own tradeoffs, not to be smuggled in through deployment. Multiple catalogs on one host (long-term plan section 6). A CDN or WAF (see Public exposure), an alerting system beyond the checks in bd-n7a.4 (backup freshness, uptime, instance status, CPU burst), and any second instance.

## Findings the brief did not anticipate

- Production serves no media today; the media decision precedes the first deploy.
- Django's default logging drops production errors: the console handler is DEBUG-only and request errors go to an unconfigured `mail_admins`. `check --deploy` also reports the proxy header and secure-cookie settings unset, and gunicorn's `--forwarded-allow-ips` must name the Docker bridge, not `127.0.0.1`, when Caddy is on the host. One settings ticket covers these and is platform-neutral.
- The Dockerfile's `DATABASE_URL` line is dead: settings read `DATA_DIR`. `collectstatic` does not open the database, so the build is unaffected, but the runtime guard above matters.
- Lightsail has no instance roles; this is the one security tradeoff of the recommendation.
- Litestream 0.5 defaults to 24 h retention.
- A drill instance running the production entrypoint would replicate into the production replica path; the entrypoint needs an off switch.
- `docs/deployment.md` has been empty since bd-mej; the deploy ticket writes it.
- PR #39 (stylesheet built in the image) and PR #37 (`manage.py reindex`) have both merged: the image needs nothing from the deploy, and the drill has a command for rebuilding the index.
- The `AWS_*` placeholders in `.env.example` become live in the media and Litestream tickets and their "no code reads these" note goes.

## Implementation tickets

Production starts with an empty database; a rebuild from any backup (latest, a moment in the last seven days, or a dated snapshot) is `just rebuild`. Configuration is written by `just configure`, which asks the owner only for the site password, the Anthropic key and the ping URLs.

In order. bd-n7a.1 and bd-n7a.2 are application changes that can be done now and hold on any platform; bd-n7a.3 is the image and holds on any Docker host; bd-n7a.4 is the only platform-specific ticket; bd-n7a.5 needs the four before it; bd-n7a.6 needs bd-n7a.5.

1. bd-n7a.1: production settings behind a TLS-terminating proxy.
2. bd-n7a.2: media in S3 through a storage backend selected by environment.
3. bd-n7a.3: Litestream replication, daily snapshots and `just rebuild` in the image.
   bd-99s3: rehearse the whole deployment locally with the real image and `deploy/` files, before anything is provisioned.
4. bd-n7a.4: provision the Lightsail instance, buckets and IAM user with a script.
5. bd-n7a.5: publish the image from CI and deploy it with `just deploy` over SSH.
6. bd-n7a.6: run a restore onto a throwaway instance and record the result.

Application changes that also precede the first deploy, platform-neutral like bd-n7a.1: bd-aau2 (the site password gate in front of the login pages, and the QR handoff through it) and bd-se7v (robots and noindex), both blocking bd-n7a.5; bd-nkfo (the site time zone). After the first deploy, on the host: bd-dovi (the scheduled staging sweep, which needs bd-n7a.2) and bd-2a1e (clearing expired sessions).
notes: Plan reviewed against the code on 2026-09-22. Decisions: Lightsail in us-east-1, hostname otzar.onebiglibrary.net (DNS managed by the owner outside AWS), gunicorn gthread workers, django-axes for login throttling, IAM key restricted by aws:SourceIp, and images built in CI but deployed from the owner's machine with just deploy rather than on every merge. Review findings are folded into bd-n7a.1, .3, .4 and .5. Public exposure decided on 2026-09-23: the site password gate in front of the login pages, robots and noindex, a request size cap, a burst alarm, and maintenance and lockdown switches; no Cloudflare, no CloudFront or WAF for now. On 2026-09-23: production starts empty and rebuilds go through just rebuild; configuration through just configure and just env-set; deploy/ ships with each deploy; a local rehearsal (bd-99s3) precedes provisioning, with moto server as the S3 stand-in since MinIO's community repository is archived.

title: Configure Django for production behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy
description:
The container runs behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS (Caddy on the instance, per bd-n7a). Django sees plain HTTP from the proxy, so in production `request.is_secure()` is False, the session and CSRF cookies are sent without the Secure flag, and `manage.py check --deploy` reports W004 (HSTS), W012 (`SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE`) and W016 (`CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE`). The QR handoff in `ingest/views.py` works around the scheme problem by inferring https from `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS`; once the proxy header is trusted that inference is unnecessary but harmless.

A second gap: Django's default logging sends the `django` logger to the console only while `DEBUG` is true and routes request errors to `mail_admins`, which is not configured. A 500 in production therefore leaves nothing but gunicorn's access-log line.

## Changes

All in `otzar/settings.py`, keyed on `DEBUG` being false so local development is unchanged:

- `SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO", "https")`. This is safe only when every request reaches gunicorn through the proxy. In the deployment gunicorn listens on the Docker network and only Caddy can reach it; say so in a comment next to the setting, because the setting is a vulnerability on any host where gunicorn is reachable directly.
- `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True`, `CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True`.
- `SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS`: pick a value and record the choice. A short one (an hour) is safe to start with and can be raised once the site has served https for a while; or leave HSTS to Caddy, which does not set it by default. Either is fine; the point is a deliberate decision rather than the warning.
- Leave `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT` off. Caddy redirects http to https itself; W008 stays and is expected.
- `LOGGING`: the application loggers (`catalog`, `ingest`, `sources`) already have a console handler. The `django` logger does not: its handler in `DEFAULT_LOGGING` carries `require_debug_true`, so with `DEBUG` false a request traceback goes only to `mail_admins`. Add `django` and `django.request` to the dict with the existing console handler, active regardless of `DEBUG`, so tracebacks reach the container's stdout where `docker compose logs` collects them.
- `SECRET_KEY`: the setting falls back to a hardcoded development key. With `DEBUG` false and `SECRET_KEY` unset or equal to that fallback, raise `ImproperlyConfigured` at startup rather than sign sessions with a key published in the repository.
- `entrypoint.sh`: gunicorn's `--forwarded-allow-ips` defaults to `127.0.0.1`, which is the proxy's address only when both run in the same network namespace. With Caddy on the host and gunicorn in a container the request arrives from the Docker bridge address, and gunicorn strips the forwarded headers before Django sees them. Read the value from an environment variable (`FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS`) that the deployment sets.
- `entrypoint.sh`: switch gunicorn from two sync workers to `--worker-class gthread --workers 2 --threads 4`. OCR (a vision call with up to 8192 output tokens) and the SRU cascade (a 3 s delay between catalog requests) both run inside the request, so with sync workers two slow requests occupy the whole server and every other page waits. Threads share the process's SQLite connections per thread, which WAL mode and the 5 s busy timeout already handle; eight concurrent requests fit in 1 GB. Keep `--timeout 120`; under gthread it bounds a stuck worker rather than a slow request.
- Remove the password reset routes. `django.contrib.auth.urls` mounts `/accounts/password_reset/` and its three follow-on views; the admin's fallback templates render them, and no email backend is configured, so submitting the form raises. Include only `login` and `logout`. An administrator resets a password through the admin.
- Add `django-axes` to limit password guessing on `/accounts/login/` and `/admin/login/`. Lock by the combination of username and IP address (`AXES_LOCKOUT_PARAMETERS = [["username", "ip_address"]]`) after five failures for one hour, so one person mistyping does not lock out everyone behind the same address. Axes reads the client address from `REMOTE_ADDR`, which behind Caddy is the Docker bridge; configure `AXES_IPWARE_PROXY_COUNT = 1` and `AXES_IPWARE_META_PRECEDENCE_ORDER = ["HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR"]` so it sees the real client. `AxesStandaloneBackend` goes first in `AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS` and `AxesMiddleware` last in `MIDDLEWARE`; its tables go through migrations. The lockout page states the wait and names no username. `manage.py axes_reset` clears a lockout; `docs/administration.md` says so.
- `SitePasswordMiddleware` compares the submitted password with `==`. Use `hmac.compare_digest`. Axes does not cover this form, since it is not a Django authentication; the site password is a shared gate for the public pages, not an account, and throttling it is left out deliberately.

## Tests

Unit tests: with `DEBUG=false` the settings resolve as above; a request carrying `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` is `is_secure()`; the QR handoff URL built from such a request starts with `https://`; startup refuses a missing or fallback `SECRET_KEY` when `DEBUG` is false; `/accounts/password_reset/` returns 404. E2e: a login that fails five times with one username shows the lockout page, and a correct password for a different username from the same browser still logs in.

## Platform

None. This applies on any host where a proxy fronts the container. It has to land before the first deploy.
close_reason: Production settings, gthread, django-axes, SECRET_KEY guard, password reset removal and django logging

title: Store media in S3 through a storage backend selected by environment
description:
`MEDIA_ROOT` is `DATA_DIR/media`, and `otzar/urls.py` mounts `/media/` only when `DEBUG` is true. A production deployment today serves no images at all: `ScanResult.image.url` and `TitlePageImage.image.url` render to `/media/...` paths that nothing answers. Something has to serve media before the first deploy. bd-n7a recommends S3 through Django's storage API rather than the instance disk; the reasoning and the alternative are recorded there.

What the code already does right: every access goes through the storage API. OCR reads the photo with `scan.image.open("rb")`, discard removes it with `scan.image.delete()`, templates use `.url`; nothing reads `.path`. So this is a dependency and a settings switch, not application code.

## Changes

- Add `django-storages[s3]` (which brings `boto3`) to the dependencies.
- In `otzar/settings.py`, when `AWS_S3_MEDIA_BUCKET` is set, configure `STORAGES["default"]` as `storages.backends.s3.S3Storage` with the bucket and region, `file_overwrite` off, a private default ACL, and query-string authentication on, so `.url` yields a presigned URL (default expiry 3600 s) and objects are reachable only through URLs the app hands out. When the variable is unset, keep `FileSystemStorage`: local development, CI and both test suites do not change.
- Credentials: `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` from the environment, which boto3 reads on its own; on a host with an instance role they can be omitted. `.env.example` and the configuration table in `docs/administration.md` say no code reads the `AWS_*` variables; after this ticket the media bucket variable is read, and the backup bucket variables are read by the Litestream ticket. Rewrite both to describe what each variable does.
- Keep the upload paths as they are (`staging/YYYY/MM/DD/<uuid>.jpg`, `title-pages/YYYY/MM/DD/`, `covers/YYYY/MM/DD/`). The backend adds no prefix. The provisioning ticket turns on versioning and a 30-day noncurrent-version expiry on the bucket; that is the media backup.
- `cleanup_staging` finds orphans by walking `Path(settings.MEDIA_ROOT) / "staging"` with `rglob`, ages them by `stat().st_mtime` and removes them with `unlink()` (`staging_files` and `_delete_orphans`). On S3 that directory does not exist, `staging_files` returns at its `is_dir()` check, and the orphan half of the sweep reports nothing and deletes nothing without an error. Rewrite both through `default_storage`: recurse with `listdir`, age with `get_modified_time`, remove with `delete`. The discarded-row half already goes through `scan.image.delete()`. Test the orphan sweep against `InMemoryStorage` or `moto`, since a test that points `MEDIA_ROOT` at a temporary directory passes whether or not the code goes through the storage API.
- bd-yg9 moves a file from staging to its permanent path. Through the storage API a move is read, save, delete; on S3 that is a copy and a delete. No special handling.
- `AWS_S3_ENDPOINT_URL` works only if `settings.py` reads it from the environment into the setting of the same name; django-storages reads Django settings, not the environment. Do that, and list it in `.env.example` as optional.
- Rewrite the media lines of "Backup and restore" in `docs/administration.md`: with the bucket set, media is not under `DATA_DIR`, its backup is bucket versioning with a 30-day noncurrent window, and recovering a deleted or overwritten image means restoring the noncurrent version with an administrator identity, since the instance key has no `s3:GetObjectVersion`.
- `_ocr_results.html` links "Open full-size image" to `scan.image.url`; with a 3600 s expiry that link returns AccessDenied on a review page left open longer than an hour. Raise `querystring_expire`, or state the limit in the user guide.

## Tests

Unit tests for the settings switch (variable set and unset) and for the storage class and URL shape. The S3 code path is not exercised by CI. If a round-trip test (save, open, delete) with `moto` stays under a few dozen lines, add it; otherwise the deploy ticket's smoke test covers it: upload a title-page photo on the deployed site and confirm the image renders. E2e: N/A, no user-visible change on local storage.

Pin `STORAGES["default"]` to `FileSystemStorage` in an autouse fixture in `tests/conftest.py`, the way `isolated_response_cache` pins the cache. `settings.py` calls `load_dotenv()`, so a developer `.env` carrying `AWS_S3_MEDIA_BUCKET` (which the Litestream ticket's scratch-bucket check invites) would otherwise switch the suite to S3, and the tests that isolate media by setting `MEDIA_ROOT` would write to the bucket or fail under pytest-socket.

## Alternative

Media on the instance disk: no Python change; Caddy serves `/media/*` with `file_server` rooted at `DATA_DIR/media`; a timer runs `aws s3 sync` hourly into the versioned bucket; the restore drill gains a sync-back step; the instance disk becomes a second system of record. If the owner prefers this, this ticket becomes a Caddy block and a timer in the provisioning ticket, and the storage-API discipline still holds.

## Platform

None. Only the bucket is AWS, and any S3-compatible endpoint works through `AWS_S3_ENDPOINT_URL`.
close_reason: Media on S3 through django-storages when a bucket is set; staging sweep through the storage API

title: Replicate the database to S3 with Litestream and take daily snapshots
description:
Two mechanisms, as bd-n7a lays out: continuous replication, which covers losing the machine, and dated snapshots, which cover a mistake noticed later. Both live in the container image, so they work on any Docker host with a local disk. Nothing here is Lightsail-specific.

## Image

The image this ticket extends has three faults to fix first, since every later check runs against it.

- Dev dependencies are installed. `uv sync --frozen --no-dev` builds the environment without them, and then `uv run` re-syncs the default groups, which include `dev`: verified by syncing with `--no-dev` and running `uv run python -c pass`, which installed forty packages including pytest, playwright and ruff. The Dockerfile's `tailwind build` step does this at build time, and the entrypoint's `uv run` would do it at container start on any image where the build had not. Set `ENV UV_NO_DEV=1` (or put `/app/.venv/bin` on `PATH` and call the executables directly), and confirm with `uv pip list` in the built image that no dev package is present.
- The image does not know its commit. `.dockerignore` excludes `.git`, so `build_info.resolve()` returns None, the footer shows no commit, and the snapshot manifest below would record none. Accept a `GIT_COMMIT` build argument, set it as an environment variable, and have `build_info` read it before trying git. The CI image job passes the SHA it built; a local build without the argument reports nothing, as the module's docstring already promises for a tree without git metadata.
- Pin the `uv` image (`ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:<version>`, not `latest`) so a rebuild of the same commit gets the same tool. Add `studies/` (about 30 MB, not read by the application) to `.dockerignore`.

## Litestream

- Install the Litestream release binary in the image and pin the version. 0.5.x replaced the WAL-segment format with LTX; the keys below are 0.5 semantics, so check the reference for the pinned version.
- Configuration at `/etc/litestream.yml`, written by the entrypoint from the environment: one database, `${DATA_DIR}/db.sqlite3`; one replica, `s3://${AWS_S3_BACKUP_BUCKET}/${LITESTREAM_REPLICA_PATH}` in `${AWS_S3_REGION}`, where `LITESTREAM_REPLICA_PATH` defaults to `litestream/db` and changes only through `just rebuild` (below). Credentials come from the standard `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` variables, which Litestream reads itself and which fall back to an instance role on a host that has one.
- Settings: `sync-interval` at its 1 s default; `snapshot.interval: 24h`; `snapshot.retention: 168h`, so any moment in the last seven days is restorable with `-timestamp`. The default retention is 24 h, which is too short to be useful for a mistake noticed the next day. Leave `l0-retention` at its default.
- Entrypoint order. First, refuse to start when `DATA_DIR` is unset or resolves to `/app`: an unset `DATA_DIR` runs against the image's own filesystem, and the next redeploy discards the catalog. The Dockerfile's `DATABASE_URL` line is dead (settings read `DATA_DIR`) and can go at the same time. Second, `litestream restore -if-db-not-exists -if-replica-exists -o "$DATA_DIR/db.sqlite3" <replica>`, so a fresh disk pulls the latest copy before migrate runs. Third, `litestream replicate -exec "<migrate, then gunicorn>"`, so replication is running while migrations write. Litestream exits when the child exits.
- An environment switch (`LITESTREAM_DISABLED=1` or an empty bucket variable) that skips both Litestream steps and runs the child directly. The restore drill needs it: a drill instance that runs the production entrypoint would replicate into the production replica path.
- Local check before merging: run the image against a scratch bucket (or the local rehearsal's S3 stand-in, bd-99s3), create a record, and confirm LTX objects appear under the replica path.

## Rebuilding from a backup

A rebuild is the same procedure whether the instance is the same one after a bad migration or a new one after losing the machine: `just rebuild`, which runs `deploy/rebuild.sh` on the instance, with exactly one of:

- `--latest`: the replica's current state;
- `--at <time>`: the replica's state at that moment, within its seven-day retention (`litestream restore -timestamp`);
- `--snapshot <date>`: a dated snapshot from `snapshots/` (35 days) or `monthly/` (13 months).

In order: stop the app container; move the current database and its `-wal` and `-shm` files aside under `DATA_DIR/pre-rebuild/<timestamp>/` rather than deleting them; restore into place; set `LITESTREAM_REPLICA_PATH` in `.env` to a new path, `litestream/db-<UTC timestamp of the rebuild>`; start the app; print the record count, the newest record's creation time and the replica path now in use.

The new replica path is what makes a rebuild to an earlier point safe. Resuming replication into the old path would write the older database over the history that came after it, which is exactly the history needed if the chosen point turns out to be the wrong one. The old path is left in place and expires under the bucket's lifecycle rules; `--at` and `--latest` take `--from <path>` to restore from it while it lasts. The snapshot command's freshness check and bd-n7a.5's `just backup-status` read `LITESTREAM_REPLICA_PATH`, so they follow the current path. Whether Litestream 0.5 would itself refuse or detect writing an older database into a newer replica is not relied on; the restore drill records what it does.

Images are not rolled back and do not need to be. They stay in the media bucket; a restored record points at a key that still exists unless its image was deleted more than 30 days before. Images uploaded after the restore point are left unreferenced: the staging sweep removes staged ones, and confirmed title pages stay in the bucket.

The first production start is a rebuild of nothing: the replica is empty, the entrypoint's `-if-replica-exists` restore does nothing, and `migrate` creates an empty database. Production starts empty; local development data is not carried over.

## Daily snapshot

- A management command (`snapshot_db` or similar) that copies the live database with `sqlite3.Connection.backup()`, the online-backup API, which is safe against a WAL database in use, to a temporary file under `DATA_DIR`; gzips it; uploads it with boto3 to `s3://<backup bucket>/snapshots/YYYY/MM/DD/db.sqlite3.gz`; and writes `manifest.json` beside it holding the record count, the commit from `settings.BUILD_INFO`, and the timestamp. On the first of the month it also copies the pair to `monthly/YYYY/MM/`. It writes `snapshots/latest.json` (same content) so backup freshness is one GET.
- The command also checks replication: it lists the replica path and reads the age of the newest object under `litestream/`. When the upload succeeded and that age is under an hour, it GETs the URL in `BACKUP_PING_URL` (a dead-man's switch at healthchecks.io or similar, configured by the provisioning ticket); on any failure it GETs the same URL with `/fail` appended and exits non-zero. An unset `BACKUP_PING_URL` skips the ping. The service raises an alert when a success ping is late, so a timer that stops firing, a snapshot that fails and a Litestream process that has died all reach a person without anyone reading a log.
- Scheduling is the host's job: a systemd timer (or cron) runs `docker compose exec app python manage.py snapshot_db` daily. The provisioning ticket installs the timer. The deploy script runs the same command before pulling a new image; that snapshot is the rollback point for a bad migration.
- Lifecycle rules on the bucket, set by the provisioning ticket: `snapshots/` expires after 35 days, `monthly/` after 400 days, `litestream/` is left to Litestream's own retention. The bucket is versioned, so an expiry or a Litestream delete leaves a noncurrent version behind; the provisioning ticket also expires noncurrent versions after 30 days. At this catalog's size the storage is cents a month.
- Not backed up, on purpose: `DATA_DIR/cache` (derived from the database) and `staticfiles` (built into the image).

## Docs and tests

The backup section of `docs/administration.md` describes the two mechanisms, what each protects against, and the retention windows. The restore procedure moves to the write-up the restore drill ticket produces. A unit test runs the snapshot command against local storage with the S3 client stubbed and checks the manifest, the success ping, and the failure ping when the replica is stale. A unit test covers `build_info` reading `GIT_COMMIT`.

Add `AWS_S3_BACKUP_BUCKET`, `AWS_S3_REGION`, `BACKUP_PING_URL`, `LITESTREAM_DISABLED` and `LITESTREAM_REPLICA_PATH` to `.env.example` and the configuration table in `docs/administration.md`, each with what reads it. `BACKUP_PING_URL` is a credential in effect: anyone holding it can send the success ping and silence the alert. The Litestream path and `just rebuild` are exercised end to end by the local rehearsal (bd-99s3) and verified against AWS by the restore drill, not by unit tests.
