title: Provision the Lightsail instance, S3 buckets and IAM user with a script
description:
The platform-specific ticket. bd-n7a recommends Lightsail; if the owner chooses EC2 instead, this is the ticket that changes (instance creation, an instance role instead of an IAM user, EBS snapshots through Data Lifecycle Manager instead of Lightsail's automatic snapshots), and the other tickets in the set stay as they are.

## Before provisioning

Done by the owner in the console, before the script runs:

- AWS account: MFA on the root user; an administrator identity (IAM Identity Center or an IAM user with MFA) for running the script, never root access keys; an AWS Budgets alert by email at $20 a month.
- Anthropic console: a monthly spend limit on the key the instance will hold. `OCR_DAILY_CALL_CAP` bounds a retry loop inside the application; the console limit bounds a leaked key.
- healthchecks.io: an account, and the checks bd-n7a.4's alerting section lists (backup freshness, uptime; later the staging sweep). Their ping URLs are entered at `just configure`.
- Outbound catalog access from AWS. Some catalogs throttle or block cloud address ranges, and the LC endpoint is plain http on port 210. Before building the rest, launch the instance (or any throwaway instance in the region) and run one request with `curl` against NLI, LC (plain http, port 210), DNB, VIAF, `covers.openlibrary.org` and `api.anthropic.com`, and against K10plus where bd-55ta adds it. A block here is the one risk in this plan that code cannot fix, and it changes the plan if it happens.

## Deliverable

`scripts/provision.sh`, driven by the AWS CLI with one region variable and an explicit `--profile` (it never falls back to the default profile, so it cannot provision into the wrong account), idempotent where the API allows, plus the provisioning section of `docs/deployment.md`. A shell script rather than Terraform: one instance, two buckets and one user do not justify a state file to store and a second tool to learn, and the script is the record of what exists. The script stops where an operator has to type a secret.

## Instance

- Lightsail, the 1 GB / 2 vCPU / 40 GB dual-stack Linux bundle ($7 a month), Ubuntu 24.04 LTS blueprint, in us-east-1. The root disk persists across stop and start and is what snapshots capture; a separate block-storage disk is not needed at this size.
- A static IP attached to the instance. Firewall: 22 (key-only SSH), 80, 443. The owner's own public key is imported with `aws lightsail import-key-pair` and named at launch, so SSH uses the key the owner already has rather than one downloaded from Lightsail.
- After attaching the static IP, the script prints it and polls DNS until `otzar.onebiglibrary.net` resolves to it, and only then lets Caddy start, so the first certificate request cannot fail on DNS.
- Security updates: unattended-upgrades is on in the Ubuntu image; set `Automatic-Reboot "true"` with a reboot time in the early morning, so kernel updates take effect without a login. The container comes back through its restart policy and Caddy through systemd.
- Automatic snapshots on: daily, seven kept, about $0.05 per GB-month of snapshot data. These roll back the machine (OS, Docker, Caddy, `.env`), not the catalog; the catalog's backups are in S3.
- A launch script (user data) that installs Docker with the Compose plugin, Caddy, and the AWS CLI; creates a 1 GB swap file; creates `/opt/otzar` with the contents of the repo's `deploy/` directory (`compose.yml`, `Caddyfile`, `deploy.sh`, `rebuild.sh`, the timer units); bd-n7a.5 keeps them current on every deploy, and `/opt/otzar/data` as `DATA_DIR`.
- `compose.yml`: one service, the GHCR image, `DATA_DIR` bind-mounted, port 8000 published on 127.0.0.1 only, `restart: unless-stopped`, a named network with a fixed subnet (`172.30.0.0/24`, gateway `172.30.0.1`) so the address Caddy's requests arrive from is known in advance and `FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS` is the constant `172.30.0.1` rather than whatever Docker picks, and the `json-file` log driver with `max-size: 10m` and `max-file: 5`. Docker keeps container logs without limit by default. The rotation size is also the answer to how long request data (ISBNs, record identifiers, search queries) stays in the logs: a few weeks of light use, then gone. `Caddyfile`: the site hostname, `request_body { max_size 15MB }`, and `reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8000`. Caddy obtains the certificate from Let's Encrypt and redirects http to https. The body limit matters because Django streams an uploaded file to temporary disk with no size cap of its own; the browser already resizes a photo to 1500 px before upload, so 15 MB leaves ample room for a legitimate one. The site block imports `/opt/otzar/maintenance.caddy`, which is empty in normal running and holds a `respond` returning a static 503 page when maintenance is on (bd-n7a.5's `just maintenance`); `/health/` is left out of that response so the uptime check keeps reporting the application itself.
- DNS: the hostname is `otzar.onebiglibrary.net`, managed by the owner outside AWS, so there is no Route 53 cost. Create an A record to the static IP with a 300 s TTL, and confirm it resolves before Caddy first starts: Caddy requests the certificate on start, and repeated failed validations hit Let's Encrypt's failed-validation rate limit. No AAAA record: the static IP is IPv4 only, and the instance's IPv6 address changes when the instance is relaunched from a snapshot, which is the upgrade path below.
- Upgrade path, for the docs: Lightsail cannot resize in place. Snapshot, launch the 2 GB bundle from the snapshot, move the static IP. About fifteen minutes of downtime.

## S3

Two buckets in the instance's region, both with public access blocked and versioning on: a media bucket (served by the app through presigned URLs) and a backup bucket (never served). Lifecycle: media noncurrent versions expire after 30 days; on the backup bucket, `snapshots/` after 35 days and `monthly/` after 400 days, with `litestream/` left alone, and noncurrent versions of every prefix expire after 30 days. On a versioned bucket an expiry or a delete only adds a delete marker; without the noncurrent rule, Litestream's own deletes accumulate and the bucket grows without limit. Two buckets rather than prefixes because the media bucket is reachable through the app and the backup bucket must never be.

## IAM

Lightsail instances cannot assume an instance role, so the box holds a static access key. One IAM user (`otzar-instance`) with one inline policy allowing `s3:ListBucket`, `s3:GetObject`, `s3:PutObject` and `s3:DeleteObject` on exactly the two buckets (Litestream deletes expired files, so `DeleteObject` is required). The policy has two statements. The first allows `s3:GetObject` on the media bucket with no address condition: every image reaches the browser through a presigned URL signed by this user, S3 evaluates the signer's policy against the address the browser connects from, and an `aws:SourceIp` condition on that action would refuse every image to every visitor. The second allows `s3:ListBucket`, `s3:PutObject` and `s3:DeleteObject` on both buckets and `s3:GetObject` on the backup bucket, with `aws:SourceIp` equal to the static IP. A leaked key can then read media from anywhere, which presigning already allows, but cannot write, delete, or read backups from anywhere but the instance. The policy does not grant `s3:DeleteObjectVersion`: someone holding the key can hide objects behind delete markers but not remove versions, and the 30-day noncurrent window is how long they stay recoverable. One access key, written into `/opt/otzar/.env` (root, mode 0600) and nowhere else. Document rotation: create a second key, replace it in `.env`, restart, delete the first. A second, read-only user for the restore drill, created by the drill ticket.

## Secrets

`/opt/otzar/.env` holds `SECRET_KEY`, `DEBUG=false`, `ALLOWED_HOSTS`, `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS`, `DATA_DIR`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `CLAUDE_MODEL`, `OCR_DAILY_CALL_CAP`, `SITE_PASSWORD`, `RECORD_ID_PREFIX`, `TIME_ZONE`, `FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS`, `BACKUP_PING_URL`, `AWS_S3_MEDIA_BUCKET`, `AWS_S3_BACKUP_BUCKET`, `AWS_S3_REGION`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, plus `STAGING_RETENTION_DAYS` and `STAGING_SWEEP_PING_URL` once bd-dovi lands. `SITE_PASSWORD` is required in this deployment: it is the gate in front of the login pages (bd-aau2), and the system check that bead adds warns when it is empty. It is written by `just configure`, not by hand. Of its variables, most are known without asking:

- generated: `SECRET_KEY`;
- fixed in the template: `DEBUG=false`, `DATA_DIR`, `TIME_ZONE=America/New_York`, `CLAUDE_MODEL`, `OCR_DAILY_CALL_CAP`, `RECORD_ID_PREFIX`, `FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS`, `LITESTREAM_REPLICA_PATH`;
- derived from the hostname: `ALLOWED_HOSTS`, `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS`;
- produced by the provisioning script: the bucket names, the region, and the access key and secret, passed straight from the IAM step into the file and never printed.

`just configure` prompts only for `SITE_PASSWORD`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and the ping URLs, with input hidden, and writes the file to the instance as root, mode 0600. Those prompted values are the whole of what the owner keeps in a password manager to rebuild the file; everything else is regenerated or re-derived, and a regenerated `SECRET_KEY` costs only the current sessions. `docs/deployment.md` lists them.

Later changes go through `just env-set KEY=value` (bd-n7a.5), which edits the file and recreates the container: a plain restart does not re-read an `env_file`. GitHub never holds application secrets. A Lightsail snapshot includes the file, which is acceptable inside one account.

## Deploy access

GitHub holds no credential for the instance. CI pushes images to GHCR, which is public, so the instance pulls without logging in; deploys run from the owner's machine over the owner's own SSH login (the key registered with Lightsail at launch, or one added to `authorized_keys` by the launch script), which uses `sudo` to run `/opt/otzar/deploy.sh`. There is no separate deploy user or deploy key. Record the instance's host key from the Lightsail console on first boot and compare it on first connection, rather than accepting whatever answers. Password authentication is off in the blueprint.

## First start and verification

`docker compose up -d` once through `just deploy` on the first image (`deploy.sh` treats a host with no running container as a first deploy and skips the pre-deploy snapshot); `createsuperuser` through `docker compose exec`. Then: `https://<hostname>/health/` returns 200 from outside; the certificate is valid; after creating one record, LTX objects appear under `litestream/` in the backup bucket. Record the instance name, static IP, bucket names and region in `docs/deployment.md`.

Production starts empty. Local development data is not carried over; the first start creates an empty database, and the first account is made with `just manage createsuperuser`. Rebuilding production from a backup later is `just rebuild` (bd-n7a.3).

`docs/deployment.md` does not exist; this ticket creates it and adds it to `nav` in `mkdocs.yml`. The docs site is published to GitHub Pages from `main`, so the page is public: record the hostname, region and instance name there, and keep the healthchecks.io URLs and the access key ID out of it.

## Timers and teardown

The host's scheduled jobs (the snapshot, and later the staging sweep and session clearing) run through one systemd template, `otzar-task@.service` with a `.timer` per job, each running `docker compose exec app python manage.py <job>` and logging to the journal under its own name. A new job is a new timer file in `deploy/`, not a new hand-written unit.

`scripts/teardown.sh` deletes an instance the script created (and, with a flag, its static IP), refusing to touch the production instance unless named explicitly. The restore drill uses it for the throwaway instance.

## Alerting

Nobody watches this machine, so failures have to reach the owner on their own.

- Backups: a check at healthchecks.io (free tier) expecting one ping a day with a two-hour grace period. `snapshot_db` pings it on success and on failure, and treats a stale Litestream replica as a failure. The URL goes in `.env` as `BACKUP_PING_URL`.
- Availability: an HTTP check on `https://otzar.onebiglibrary.net/health/` every five minutes from the same service or any free uptime monitor, alerting after two consecutive failures. It also catches an expired certificate.
- The machine: a Lightsail metric alarm on the instance status check, notifying by email.
- Load: a Lightsail metric alarm on `BurstCapacityPercentage` below 25%. The bundle is burstable: sustained load spends its CPU credits and then throttles the instance to its baseline for everyone. This alarm is the signal that unwanted traffic is costing real capacity, and the cue to reach for the switches in bd-n7a.5.

When bd-dovi schedules the staging sweep, it adds a check of the same kind as the backup one. All of them notify the owner's email. The provisioning section of `docs/deployment.md` lists them and what each one means when it fires.

## Cost

About $7 a month for the instance, under $1 for snapshots and S3 combined. bd-n7a has the comparison with EC2.

No lifecycle rule covers litestream/, and Litestream prunes only the path it is writing to, so an old path stays until the owner removes it with an administrator identity: aws s3 rm --recursive s3://<backup bucket>/<old path>/ (docs/administration.md, rebuild section; rebuild.sh prints the old path). title: Publish the image from CI and deploy it from the operator's machine
description:
CI builds the image for every commit on `main`; the owner deploys it from their own machine with `just deploy`. Merging and deploying are separate steps: a merge publishes an image, and a deploy puts one on the instance when the owner chooses.

## Why not continuous deployment

Deploying on every merge needs a credential in GitHub that can reach the instance and run a root script there, and with it a deploy user, a forced command, a `production` environment and host-key pinning in the workflow. Deploying entirely from the owner's machine removes that credential but builds an x86 image under emulation on Apple silicon and lets an untested tree reach production. Building in CI and deploying from the laptop keeps the useful half of each: the image is built from the commit CI tested, on a native runner, and GitHub never holds anything that can touch the instance. What it gives up is deploy-on-merge, which a single maintainer does not need; production may trail `main` until the next deploy, and the footer's commit says which image is running.

## Image job

A `publish-image` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with `needs: [lint, test, test-e2e]` and `if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`, so it runs only after every required check has passed on that commit, and never on a pull request. It grants itself `packages: write` at job level; the workflow-level `contents: read` stays for every other job. Steps: check out with `persist-credentials: false`; build for `linux/amd64` with `--build-arg GIT_COMMIT=${{ github.sha }}`; tag `ghcr.io/dchud/otzar:<full sha>` and `:main`; push with `GITHUB_TOKEN`. The repository is public, so the package is public and costs nothing. Pin every action by SHA as the rest of the file does; zizmor must pass on the new job.

A test job that skips its suite because the changed files cannot reach tested code still reports success, so a docs-only merge also publishes an image. That is correct: the image is a function of the commit, and the deploy chooses which one to run.

## just deploy

`just deploy [sha]`, defaulting to the head of `github-dchud/main` after a fetch; a short SHA is expanded with `git rev-parse`. Before connecting it checks, and refuses on failure:

- the SHA is on `github-dchud/main`, so an unmerged branch cannot be deployed;
- `ghcr.io/dchud/otzar:<sha>` exists (`docker manifest inspect`), which means every required check passed on it.

It deploys the image, not the working tree, so local uncommitted changes cannot leak into production and need no check. Then it runs `git archive <sha> deploy/ | ssh <host> sudo /opt/otzar/deploy.sh <sha>` with the host from `DEPLOY_HOST` in the local `.env`, and streams the output. The instance's config files therefore always come from the commit being deployed: without this, `compose.yml`, the `Caddyfile`, the timers and `deploy.sh` itself would stay as provisioning left them while the image moved on.

Alongside it: `just configure` writes the instance's `.env` (bd-n7a.4); `just env-set KEY=value` changes one variable and recreates the container, which is how the site password is rotated or the time zone changed; `just manage <command> [args]` runs a management command in the app container over SSH, for `createsuperuser`, `axes_reset_username`, `reindex` and the like; `just rebuild` restores from a backup (bd-n7a.3); `just deploy-logs` tails `docker compose logs` on the instance; `just backup-status` prints the age of the newest `litestream/` object and of `snapshots/latest.json`; `just deployed` prints the SHA in `/opt/otzar/image.env`, to compare with `main`.

## deploy.sh

Kept in the repo under `deploy/` and copied to the host by provisioning. In order: reject any argument that is not a 40-character hexadecimal SHA, since it reaches a shell running as root; unpack the `deploy/` tree from standard input into `/opt/otzar/releases/<sha>/`, and install each file that differs from what is in place, reloading Caddy when the `Caddyfile` changed and running `systemctl daemon-reload` and enabling new timers when a unit changed; if the app container is running, run `docker compose exec app python manage.py snapshot_db`, the pre-deploy snapshot and the rollback point, and if it is not (the first deploy), say so and continue; write the image tag to `/opt/otzar/image.env`, which `compose.yml` reads, so a reboot starts the same image the last deploy did; `docker compose pull` and `docker compose up -d`, after which the entrypoint finds the database in place, migrates, and starts gunicorn; poll `https://<host>/health/` for up to 60 s; print the backup ages. Any failure exits non-zero.

Migrations run automatically, as `entrypoint.sh` does today. Rollback is the restore procedure applied to the pre-deploy snapshot, then `just deploy <previous sha>`; every published tag stays in GHCR. Migrations are reviewed for being non-destructive before merge, as now.

## Secrets

GitHub holds nothing for the instance; the image job uses only `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Application secrets stay in the instance's `.env`. The deploy runs on the owner's SSH key, which lives on the owner's machine.

## Switches

Two recipes for unwanted traffic, both reversible and both run from the owner's machine:

- `just maintenance on|off` writes or empties `/opt/otzar/maintenance.caddy` on the instance and reloads Caddy (`systemctl reload caddy`, no dropped connections). On: every request except `/health/` gets a static 503 page naming the site as down for maintenance. The container, the database, Litestream and the timers keep running; nothing is lost and no deploy is needed to turn it off.
- `just lockdown on|off [addresses]` changes the Lightsail firewall with `aws lightsail put-instance-public-ports` under the owner's administrator profile. On: ports 80 and 443 accept only the listed addresses (the owner's and the catalogers', kept in the local `.env` as `LOCKDOWN_ALLOW`); port 22 is untouched. Off: 80 and 443 open to all again. Traffic from anywhere else is dropped by AWS before it reaches the instance. While it is on, Let's Encrypt cannot validate a renewal; Caddy renews thirty days before expiry, so a lockdown of days is harmless and one of weeks needs watching. The uptime check fails while it is on unless its service's addresses are listed.

`docs/deployment.md` describes both, when to use which (maintenance for anything wrong with the application, lockdown for traffic), and that the load alarm in bd-n7a.4 is the usual cue.

## Smoke test

After the first deploy, and whenever this pipeline changes: log in, scan a title page from a phone through the QR handoff, confirm the image renders (this is the S3 media path, which CI does not exercise), confirm a search returns the new record, and confirm the footer names the deployed commit. Turn each switch on and off once: the 503 page appears and clears, and with lockdown on a request from an address not listed times out. Load the record page on the phone over mobile data as well as on the laptop: a presigned URL is fetched from the viewer's address, not the instance's, so this is the check that the bucket policy admits it.

## Runbook

`docs/deployment.md` is written as one runbook in order, marking which steps are the owner's and which a script's:

1. Before provisioning (owner): the AWS administrator profile; an Anthropic workspace, key and spend limit; healthchecks.io checks; the outbound catalog check.
2. Provision (script), then the DNS record (owner); the script waits for it to resolve.
3. `just configure` (script, with the owner's secrets), then `just deploy` of the current `main`.
4. `just manage createsuperuser`, then cataloger accounts in the admin; catalogers are sent the site address, the site password and their own login.
5. Smoke test, including both switches.
6. Restore drill (bd-n7a.6), and a calendar reminder to repeat it.

It then covers routine operation: deploying, changing configuration, rotating secrets, rebuilding from a backup, and what each alert means.

## Docs

Complete `docs/deployment.md`, started by the provisioning ticket: where the instance and buckets are (pointer to the provisioning script), how an image is published and how a deploy happens, how to roll back, where secrets live and how to rotate them, how to read logs, and how to tell which commit is deployed. Update "Applying code updates" in `docs/administration.md` to point at `just deploy` rather than a `git pull`.

Rewrite "Creating user accounts" in `docs/administration.md` for the deployed site: the command-line form becomes `docker compose exec app python manage.py createsuperuser` on the instance, and cataloger accounts are created in the admin.

## Platform

The SSH target is any Docker host with the compose files in place; only the address is Lightsail's.

## Tests

The first deploy exercises the path. Run `shellcheck` over `deploy.sh` in `scripts/check.sh` if it is cheap to add. E2e: N/A.

List LOCKDOWN_ALLOW beside it, and mark both as read on the owner's machine by just recipes, not by the app.

title: Run a restore from S3 onto a throwaway instance and record the result
description:
The deliverable bd-n7a names: a restore that has been executed and verified, not described. Until this has been run once, the backups are unverified.

## Guard

The drill instance must not touch production data. Give it a read-only IAM user (`s3:ListBucket`, `s3:GetObject` on both buckets) and set the entrypoint's replication switch off, so it cannot write into the production replica path or the media bucket. Uploads on the drill instance fail; that is expected. Do not attach the production hostname.

## Procedure

Script what can be scripted as `scripts/restore-drill.sh`; the rest goes in `docs/administration.md`.

1. Before restoring, read from production: `Record.objects.count()`, and for one record chosen at drill time its id, title, authors and identifiers. These are the values to compare against.
2. Launch a throwaway instance with the provisioning script (and remove it with `scripts/teardown.sh` at step 6) (Lightsail: a second 1 GB instance, billed by the hour, deleted at the end) with the read-only key and replication disabled.
3. Run `just rebuild` against the drill instance three times, once each with `--latest`, `--at` an hour earlier, and `--snapshot` for yesterday's date. The drill tests the procedure an owner would run in a real rebuild, not a separate set of manual steps. With replication disabled on the drill instance, the replica-path switch is recorded but nothing is written.
4. Start the container. The entrypoint migrates, which is a no-op when the image matches production.
5. Verify, recording each value:
   - Record count equals the manifest's count (path B) or production's count at step 1 (path A), allowing for records created in between and saying how many.
   - The chosen record's title, authors and identifiers match step 1.
   - `search_records("<a word from that title>")` returns that record. The FTS table and its shadow tables are in the same file, so both paths should carry the index. If the search returns nothing while the count is right, run `manage.py reindex`, search again, and record that a rebuild was needed.
   - The chosen record's image, or a `ScanResult.image`, returns 200 through the drill instance's pages. With media on S3 this needs no restore step; if the owner chose disk media, `aws s3 sync` it back first and verify.
   - `/health/` returns 200 through Caddy.
   - Backup freshness on production: the newest `litestream/` object is younger than an hour after a write, and `snapshots/latest.json` is younger than 25 hours.
6. Delete the throwaway instance.
7. Record whether restoring an earlier point would have been refused or detected by Litestream had replication been on, as bd-n7a.3 asks. Record in `docs/administration.md`: date, image commit, which snapshot and which timestamp, the counts, the record id checked, whether a reindex was needed, and elapsed time. Keep the last three entries.

## Repeating it

Repeat after any change to the entrypoint, the Litestream configuration or the snapshot command, and otherwise about quarterly. Nothing automates the reminder; the write-up should say so and the owner puts it on a calendar.

## Platform

Launching the throwaway instance is the only Lightsail-specific step. Tests: the drill is the test; unit and e2e are N/A.

comments.author: dchud
comments.text: Two things from bd-n7a.3 for this drill. (1) snapshot_db checks replication by writing one row to catalog.ReplicationProbe and waiting for a new key under the replica path (catalog/backups.py, check_replication), because Litestream 0.5 uploads only when the database changes and an object-age check would fail on any day nobody catalogs. So the freshness check in step 5 is a snapshot_db run on production, not an object age. snapshot_db skips the check when LITESTREAM_DISABLED is set, as it is on the drill instance. (2) When the entrypoint restored a database and Litestream resumed into the same replica path, Litestream logged 'detected database behind replica ... fetched latest L0 file', and the restored data was intact. This was seen in local testing, not on AWS. It bears on step 7's question of whether Litestream detects an earlier point written into the same path. rebuild.sh does not reach it because it always switches to a new path.

title: Make the deployment docs one runbook and follow each procedure verbatim
description:
The deployment's instructions are written piecemeal: bd-n7a.4 creates `docs/deployment.md`, bd-n7a.5 structures it as a runbook and rewrites "Applying code updates" in `docs/administration.md`, bd-n7a.3 rewrites "Backup and restore", and bd-n7a.6 records drill results. Each writes its part while building something else. Nothing owns whether the result reads as one procedure a person can follow from the top, or whether the steps are right when followed literally.

This ticket owns `docs/deployment.md` and the operational sections of `docs/administration.md` as one document, and proves them.

## Four procedures, one name each

- **Initial deploy**: before provisioning (the owner's accounts, keys, spend limits and checks), provisioning, the DNS record, `just configure`, the first `just deploy`, the first administrator and cataloger accounts, the smoke test including both switches.
- **Update**: `just deploy` of a commit on `main`; changing configuration with `just env-set`; rotating the site password, the Anthropic key and the instance's AWS key; rolling back a deploy to the pre-deploy snapshot and the previous image.
- **Rebuild**: `just rebuild`, on the same instance after a bad change or on a new one after losing the machine, from the latest state, a moment in the last seven days, or a dated snapshot; what happens to images; what the replica path switch means afterwards.
- **Restore one image**: recovering a deleted or overwritten image from the media bucket's noncurrent versions with an administrator identity.

Each is written as numbered steps, each step says who does it (the owner or a script) and what it prints when it worked, and the same term is used for the same thing everywhere: no "restore" in one place and "recover" in another for the same act. "Rebuild" is the whole-site procedure; "restore" is reserved for a single image or for the drill's verification step.

The page also carries the inventory of what the owner keeps in a password manager, what each alert means when it fires and which switch or procedure answers it, and where each piece lives (instance name, region, buckets, hostname), without secrets: the docs site is public.

## Done when

Each procedure has been followed verbatim from the published page by someone other than its author, with nothing supplied from memory: the local rehearsal (bd-99s3) covers what can run locally, the restore drill (bd-n7a.6) covers rebuild on AWS, and the first production deploy covers the initial procedure. Every correction found that way goes into the page, not into the person's head. Record in the page the date each procedure was last followed end to end.

## Tests

The procedures are the test. `./scripts/check.sh` builds the docs, so the page must build and pass the process-label and wrap checks. E2e: N/A.

title: Set the site time zone that the daily OCR cap and day boundaries use
description:
`TIME_ZONE = "UTC"` in `otzar/settings.py`. `APIUsageLog.calls_today` (`ingest/models.py`) counts OCR calls since `timezone.localtime()` midnight, and the OCR view refuses with "Try again after midnight." once `OCR_DAILY_CALL_CAP` is reached. Deployed, that midnight is UTC midnight: 20:00 for a cataloger in New York in summer, 03:00 in Jerusalem. The message names a time that is not the reader's.

Storage does not change: `USE_TZ = True`, so every datetime is written to the database in UTC whatever `TIME_ZONE` says, and `TIME_ZONE` decides only how times are shown and where a local day begins and ends. Changing it later moves no stored data.

Read `TIME_ZONE` from the environment with `UTC` as the default, set it to `America/New_York` in the production `.env`, and list it in `.env.example`, the configuration table in `docs/administration.md` and the `.env` list in bd-n7a.4. Keep the snapshot command's dated keys in UTC explicitly, so backup paths do not move if the site zone changes.

The same boundary decides "today" for any per-day view, including the activity view in bd-zvy.

The locale is separate: language and formats come from `LANGUAGE_CODE` (`en-us`), which this ticket leaves alone.

Tests: stored timestamps are UTC regardless of the setting; with `TIME_ZONE` set to a zone other than UTC, a call logged just before local midnight counts toward that day and one just after does not; with the variable unset, the setting is UTC.
close_reason: Done in #117: TIME_ZONE read from the environment

title: Show the queue on /ingest/ and its depth in the ingest mode bar
description:
`/ingest/` renders three cards -- Scan barcode, Photograph title page,
Enter manually -- that the ingest mode bar (commit 25f39b3) now carries
on every ingest page. The cards duplicate the bar directly above them,
and the only thing left that is unique to the page is a "Review queue"
link.

Two changes, one dependent on the other:

`/ingest/` renders the queue itself. The route choice is already in the
bar, so the landing page can show what is waiting rather than repeating
the navigation. `/ingest/queue/` keeps working and renders the same
view.

The mode bar gains a Queue item carrying the pending count. This is the
part that answers "did what I just scanned land?" -- right after a scan
the user is standing on `/ingest/scan/`, not on the landing page, so a
count that lives only on `/ingest/` still has to be gone looking for.
The count is per-user, matching the existing queue scoping (staff see
all).

Depends on bd-queue-rows-r91 for what the rows look like; this ticket is
about where the queue appears and how its depth is surfaced.

## Testing

E2e that `/ingest/` lists pending scans, that the bar shows a count that
tracks what is actually pending, and that the count is visible at phone
width.
close_reason: done

title: Strip MARC non-sorting delimiters from imported text
description:
Record `otzar-e` has the title `\x98The\x9c Complete Piano Etudes`.
U+0098 and U+009C are the MARC non-sorting character delimiters, which
DNB wraps around a leading article so it does not affect sort order.
Browsers render them as blank, so the title reads as though it has
stray whitespace in it.

`sources/marc.py:153` takes 245$a+$b through `get_field_value` verbatim,
and nothing downstream removes C1 control characters. Any DNB-sourced
field with a leading article carries them.

Strip the C1 range at parse time so they never reach the database, and
repair the one existing record. Worth checking whether NLI or LC use the
same convention before assuming this is DNB-only.

Found while reviewing a record in the browser during title-page work.
close_reason: Merged in PR #18

title: Render language codes as language names
description:
Language shows as the raw code -- `heb` rather than `Hebrew` -- on the
record detail page, the ingest confirm page, the scan poll partial, the
manual entry form, and in the admin filter.

## The trap

MARC 008/35-37 carries ISO 639-2/**B** bibliographic codes, so German is
`ger`, not `deu`. `sources/marc.py:197` reads exactly those bytes, and
`catalog/language_views.py:19` already stores the bibliographic form.

`pycountry` (already a dependency) indexes ISO 639-3, where these exist
only as a `bibliographic` alias:

    pycountry.languages.get(alpha_3="ger")       -> None
    pycountry.languages.get(bibliographic="ger") -> German

An alpha_3-only lookup renders German, French, Dutch, Greek, Czech,
Persian, Chinese, Romanian, Welsh, Basque, Armenian, Icelandic,
Georgian, Macedonian, Maori, Malay, Burmese, Slovak, Albanian and
Tibetan as blank -- 20 divergences. Bibliographic lookup must come
first.

## Shape

A plain module `catalog/language_codes.py` plus a template filter
library, following the existing `bidi` templatetag pattern. Shared
rather than living inside the templatetag because
`catalog/language_views.py` is a second consumer.

Two display sites render plain dicts from session/JSON rather than model
instances, so this has to be a filter, not a model property.

A small override table is needed for MARC codes withdrawn from ISO 639-2
that ISO 639-3 has since reassigned -- `gae` means Scottish Gaelic in a
pre-1997 record, but pycountry answers "Guarequena" -- plus a few codes
whose 639-3 scholarly names read oddly on a catalog page (`arc` ->
Aramaic, not "Official Aramaic (700-300 BCE)").

Do not store the display name at ingest time: the code is the
interchange value, it round-trips against `source_marc`, and a stored
name drifts when a cataloger edits the code.

## Testing

Unit tests covering the B/T divergence specifically (`ger`, `fre`,
`dut`, `gre`, `cze`, `per`), the codes this catalog actually uses
(`heb`, `yid`, `lad`, `jrb`, `jpr`, `sam`), the overrides, case and
whitespace normalization, and passthrough for unknown codes. E2e
assertions on record detail and the confirm page, including a German
record -- that is the case a naive fix renders blank.

Also fix `tests/test_views.py:18`, which sets `language="Hebrew"`, a
display name in a code field.
close_reason: Merged in PR #19

title: A failed FTS rebuild leaves the index empty and never repairs it
description:
`ensure_fts_table` decides whether to rebuild by comparing the table's columns to `FTS_COLUMNS`. Rebuilding is two steps — `rebuild_fts_table()` drops and recreates the table, then `_index_all_records()` fills it — and nothing makes them atomic.

If the second step fails, the table is left with the correct shape and no rows. Every later call compares columns, finds them matching, and returns without repopulating. Search then returns nothing, for every query, permanently, with no error.

## Reproduced

Hit on the live catalog immediately after PR #28 merged. The code was current but `catalog.0005_record_provenance` had not been applied yet, so:

1. `ensure_fts_table()` saw a 10-column table, dropped it, recreated it with 11 columns.
2. `_index_all_records()` raised `OperationalError: no such column: catalog_record.provenance`.
3. The next call saw 11 columns matching `FTS_COLUMNS` and returned immediately.
4. `search_records("Piano")` returned 0 hits where it had returned 1. The index held 0 rows against 11 records.

`reindex_all()` restored it, but nothing would have prompted anyone to run it — the failure is silent and looks like an empty catalog.

## Why it matters beyond the migration case

The migration-ordering trigger is unlikely in production, since `entrypoint.sh` migrates before starting gunicorn. But any interruption between the two steps produces the same state: a process killed mid-reindex, a deploy restarting the container, an exception on one malformed record. The index is derived data, so the cost is recoverable — but only by someone who notices, and a search returning nothing looks like a catalog problem rather than an index problem.

## Shape

Make the rebuild recoverable rather than assuming it completes. Options worth weighing: do the drop, recreate and repopulate in one transaction so a failure rolls back to the old table; or have the emptiness itself be detectable, so a table whose shape is right but whose row count is zero while records exist gets repopulated rather than trusted.

Prefer whichever keeps `ensure_fts_table` cheap — it is called on the path of every search, so it must not count rows against the record table on every query.

Worth checking whether `index_record` failing for one record during a rebuild should abort the whole thing or skip that record and report.

Found while verifying PR #28 against the live catalog.
close_reason: Merged in PR #37

title: Store, cache and manage cover images locally instead of hotlinking Open Library
description:
`RecordCover` (`catalog/models.py`) stores the bytes `fetch_cover` retrieves, through the storage API, under `covers/YYYY/MM/DD/`, with the source URL beside the file. The confirm path and `fetch_covers` both write it, and the record page renders `record.cover.image.url`. What remains is the lifecycle below, the negative-result memory, and the terms question.

## Why it is worth doing

**It stops asking a third party for the same file forever.** A cover is a static image for a book that is not going to change. Re-requesting it on every page view is the kind of thing a small catalog owes a free service not to do, and the Internet Archive is under enough load without it.

**It stops telling the Internet Archive what someone is reading.** A hotlinked image means the visitor's browser makes a request to a third party carrying their IP address and a referrer identifying the record page. For a private collection assembled in someone's home, that discloses browsing to a party the owner never chose to involve. That reason is sufficient on its own.

**It survives the source.** URLs rot, services have outages, and a cover that renders today is a broken image later with nothing held locally to fall back on.

## Shape

Keep the response body `fetch_cover_url` already has and write it through Django's storage API rather than the filesystem directly, so the path does not change when media moves to S3 under `bd-n7a.2`. The record page serves the cover from the application's own storage: local media in development, and in the deployment the media bucket through a presigned URL. That is a different origin, but it is the owner's own bucket, so the privacy argument holds. Covers share the media bucket's 30-day noncurrent rule under bd-n7a.4.

**Store them under their own prefix, separate from the collection's own images.** `media/title-pages/` and `media/staging/` hold photographs the owner took of books they hold; a cover from Open Library is a third-party file held on someone else's terms. The two want different retention, different backup and different deletion rules, and one tree cannot express that.

The operational difference is sharper than the legal one: a cover can be fetched again, and a photograph of a title page cannot be retaken once the book has been sold or the shelf rearranged. Backing both up identically means paying to preserve derivative files that can be regenerated. Under `bd-n7a.2` and `bd-n7a.3` that argues for a distinct prefix with its own lifecycle policy, or a separate bucket, and for excluding it from the snapshot that protects irreplaceable data.

Calling it a cache states the guarantee that matters: it can be emptied without losing anything, which is true here and false for everything else under `media/`.

Keep the source URL alongside the stored file rather than replacing it. It records where the image came from, which matters for attribution and for re-fetching if a stored file is lost.

**Decide the model shape against the other image work rather than alone.** `TitlePageImage` is a related model with `upload_to` and a `staged` flag; `bd-yg9` attaches it on confirm; `otzar-pbv.1` needs an image-bearing related model for bookplates, stamps and dedications. That is three tickets each adding an image attached to a record. Whether a cover is a fourth model, a row in a shared one, or an `ImageField` on `Record` is a question all four should answer the same way, and answering it once here is cheaper than answering it four times differently.

**Remember the negative result.** The lookup does not go through `sources/cache.py`, so a record with no cover is re-checked against Open Library on every backfill run. A record whose identifiers yielded nothing should say so, with enough of a timestamp that it can be retried deliberately rather than never or constantly.

`catalog/management/commands/fetch_covers.py` already walks records lacking a cover with a polite delay; it becomes download-and-store, and is the path that backfills records ingested before this lands.

## Lifecycle: the wrong cover has to be fixable

Covers will be wrong, and the reason is structural rather than occasional. Open Library is keyed on ISBN, OCLC and LCCN. ISBNs are reused across editions, small publishers reuse them across unrelated titles, a mis-transcribed check digit or a 10-versus-13 digit mismatch lands on somebody else's book, and for the reprinted Judaica sets this collection holds one ISBN routinely covers a whole multi-volume set — so every volume gets the set's cover and none of them are wrong enough to look wrong.

A cataloger looking at a record page is the person who notices. They need to act on it there, not through a database shell.

What has to exist:

- **Remove** the cover from one record, because it is the wrong book.
- **Suppress** it, so the next backfill run does not put the same wrong image back. Removal without suppression is undone on a schedule, which is worse than not offering removal. A deliberate suppression and a lookup that simply found nothing are different states and must be distinguishable — the second should be retried eventually, the first never.
- **Replace** it: with a different identifier's result, with the record's title-page image, or with a file the owner uploads. For an old Hebrew book the owner's own photograph is usually better than anything Open Library holds.
- **Refresh** one record, for the case where the stored file is damaged or the source has improved.
- **Bulk purge and re-fetch**, for a bad backfill run or a change in what the terms permit.

The single-record actions belong where the cataloger already is: the record page for the common case, with a Django admin action for the bulk path — `delete_orphans` in `catalog/admin.py` is the existing pattern. The bulk operations belong in management commands alongside `fetch_covers`.

## What has to be decided, not assumed

Open Library serves cover images sourced from several places under varying terms. Hotlinking and storing a copy are different acts, and the second is the one this ticket proposes. Establish what the terms permit for a private catalog and write the answer down, rather than inferring it from the fact that the file was already downloadable.

## Tests

Unit: removing a cover and suppressing it keeps the next backfill run from restoring it; a record whose lookup found nothing is retried while a suppressed one is not; replacing a cover with an uploaded file leaves no orphaned file behind; a successful lookup stores the file and populates the field; a 43-byte placeholder stores nothing; a timeout or HTTP error leaves the record without a cover and does not raise; a record already carrying a stored cover is not re-fetched; a record whose lookup found nothing is not re-queried on the next run.

E2e: a record page shows a cover served from local media, and makes no off-origin request while doing it; that assertion holds for `FileSystemStorage`, which the suite runs on. `tests/e2e/test_asset_delivery.py` has the pattern — abort off-origin requests through the browser context and assert none were attempted.

title: Rework the review queue into scannable rows with inline confirm
description:
The queue shows a candidate count and hides everything else behind a
Details button at the far right of each row. Deciding whether a scan
matched the right book means clicking through, and the expanded view
then offers "Use this" with little more to go on.

`_candidates.html` -- written for the title-page cascade results --
already renders the layout this needs: title/author, date,
publisher/place, series, identifiers, source, one row per candidate.
The queue's `_queue_item.html` predates it and duplicates none of it.

## Shape

Extract the candidate row markup from `_candidates.html` into a shared
partial and render it in the queue, so both surfaces stay in step.

Clicking a row expands it in place (Alpine is already in this template)
to show the full field set the record would receive -- subjects,
additional authors, identifiers, language, series -- with a Confirm
button inside the expanded row, so the decision and the action sit
together.

Each row also carries a "See full record" link that POSTs the candidate
JSON to `select_candidate`, which already stores it in session and
redirects to `/ingest/confirm/`. That is the same review page the
title-page results reach, so the queue stops being the one path that
commits without a preview. No new view is needed.

## Zero-candidate scans

A scan with no candidates currently says so only behind Details. Those
rows should say it at the top level and offer an action -- re-run the
search, or discard -- rather than expanding into an empty box.

## Prerequisite, already landed

Both confirm paths now build records through
`_create_record_from_candidate` (commit 8b4b6ca), so the inline Confirm
and the review page produce identical records. That had to come first;
before it, the queue path silently dropped `source_marc` and any date
that would not parse as an integer.

## Testing

E2e for expand-in-place, inline Confirm, and See full record reaching
`/ingest/confirm/`. The record-equivalence unit tests already exist.

title: Move the Tailwind source CSS out of the static files directory
description:
`django_tailwind_cli` raises `W001` on every management command: the Tailwind source CSS lies inside a static files directory. It is right, and the failure it predicts is a deployment failure rather than a local one.

`settings.py` sets `STATICFILES_DIRS = [BASE_DIR / "static"]` and `TAILWIND_CLI_SRC_CSS = "static/src/input.css"`, so the source file is inside the tree `collectstatic` collects. Nothing breaks today because `STORAGES["staticfiles"]` is `whitenoise.storage.CompressedStaticFilesStorage`, which compresses without resolving references.

The trap is that `CompressedManifestStaticFilesStorage` is whitenoise's recommended production backend and the obvious choice for anyone configuring production static files. It hashes filenames and rewrites references, which means it tries to resolve the `@import "tailwindcss"` inside the collected `input.css` — a directive meant for the Tailwind CLI, not for Django — and `collectstatic` fails. The person who meets this will be part-way through a deployment, reading a stack trace about a file they did not know was being collected.

There is a smaller cost being paid already: the raw Tailwind source is served at `/static/src/input.css`. Nothing needs it, and it is the only file in the static tree that is an input rather than an output.

## Shape

Move the source outside `STATICFILES_DIRS` — a sibling directory such as `assets/` keeps the input-versus-output distinction visible in the layout rather than only in the settings — and update `TAILWIND_CLI_SRC_CSS` to match. The generated `static/css/tailwind.css` stays where it is; it is an output and belongs in the collected tree.

The key-paths table in `CLAUDE.md` and the corresponding line in `AGENTS.md` name `static/src/input.css` and follow the file. `docs/development.md` should be checked for the same reference.

## Verification

`uv run python manage.py tailwind build --force` emits no `W001`, and the built stylesheet is byte-identical to the one it produces today. `uv run python manage.py collectstatic --noinput` under `CompressedManifestStaticFilesStorage` succeeds, which is the condition that actually matters and is not otherwise exercised until a deployment attempts it.
close_reason: done

title: A failed OCR re-run discards the previous extraction
description:
`run_ocr` accepts `pending` scans so the user can re-run against the
same image. On `metadata is None` it sets `ocr_output = None` and
reverts status to `awaiting_ocr` unconditionally.

So: the user has usable metadata on screen, presses "Re-run OCR" hoping
for a better read, the vision call fails transiently or returns
unparseable JSON, and the extraction they already had is gone. The edit
form is replaced by the error partial and there is no way back to it.

This is current intended behaviour --
`test_run_ocr_failure_after_success_resets_to_awaiting` asserts it, with
the rationale that the queue card should surface the scan again. The
question is whether that rationale outweighs destroying a good result on
a transient failure.

Suggested: only overwrite `ocr_output` on success, and leave a scan that
was already `pending` in `pending`. The failure notice can offer both
"Try again" and "Keep the previous result". That test would change to
assert the previous output survives.

Found in review of PR #7. Needs a decision before implementing, since it
reverses a deliberate choice.

title: Title-page scans never leave pending after a candidate is chosen
description:
Photograph a title page, run OCR, search catalogs, pick a candidate: a
Record is created and the ScanResult stays `status="pending"` with
`ocr_output` set, forever.

`title_page_poll` shows `pending` rows that have output, so the card
reappears in the "Incoming photos" pane on every device on every poll
tick, and sits in `/ingest/queue/` permanently. The pane fills with
scans that are already catalogued.

The link is dropped in the round trip. `_ocr_results.html`'s search form
posts only the metadata fields to `title_page_upload`; the response,
`_candidates.html`, has a "Use" button that posts to `select_candidate`
-> `confirm_candidate`. Nothing in that chain knows which ScanResult the
metadata came from, so nothing can mark it confirmed.

Carry `scan.id` through the search form and the candidate form, and set
`status="confirmed"`, `created_record`, and
`selected_candidate_index` when the record is created --
`confirm_scan` already does exactly this for the queue path.

Found in review of PR #7. P1 because every successful title-page ingest
leaves permanent debris in the one pane the workflow depends on.

title: Tell crawlers to stay out: robots.txt and a noindex header
description:
The deployment is a private catalog with no public audience, and nothing tells a crawler so. Search and browse are effectively unbounded for a crawler (every query and facet combination is a new URL), and behind the site password gate a crawler is shown the gate page, which it may retry indefinitely.

Serve `/robots.txt` with `User-agent: *` and `Disallow: /`, from a view exempt from the site password gate (a crawler has to be able to read it), and add `X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow` to every response through a small middleware, gate page included. Both come from the application, not from Caddy, so development and tests see what production sends.

This only stops crawlers that obey it. The others are the reason for the site password gate (bd-aau2) and the lockdown switch in bd-n7a.5.

## Tests

Unit: `/robots.txt` returns the disallow-all body with `text/plain`, with `SITE_PASSWORD` set and without logging in; a gated page, the gate page itself and `/health/` all carry the `X-Robots-Tag` header. E2e: N/A, nothing a user sees changes.
close_reason: Done in #118: robots.txt and the noindex header

title: Staged images keep a .png suffix over JPEG bytes
description:
`staging_image_path` in `ingest/models.py` allows `.png` through
`JPEG_SUFFIXES`, but the capture form re-encodes every selection to
`image/jpeg` while preserving the original filename.

Pick a PNG screenshot of a title page and it is stored at
`staging/.../<hex>.png` holding JPEG bytes, and served as
`Content-Type: image/png`. Browsers sniff past it; anything trusting the
extension or MIME type does not.

Given the unconditional re-encode, the suffix should normalise to `.jpg`
for anything that is not already `.jpg`/`.jpeg`. The docstring already
explains the re-encode, so this is a one-line change plus a test.

Found in review of PR #7.

title: Keep subject subdivisions and dedupe repeated headings
description:
The ingest confirm page shows the same subject twice.

`sources/marc.py:210-216` keeps only the first `$a` of each 650 field
and discards the subdivisions (`$v $x $y $z`), with no deduplication.
That produces visually identical entries two ways, both routine:

- Subdivided headings collapse. `650 _0 $a Jews $z Israel $x History.`
  and `650 _0 $a Jews $x Social life and customs.` both emit `Jews`.
- Parallel vocabularies repeat. LC records carry an LCSH `650 _0 $a
  Judaism.` alongside a FAST `650 _7 $a Judaism. $2 fast`; the `$2` is
  invisible here, so the list holds the heading twice.

Reproduced against a synthetic LC-shaped record: five 650 fields yielded
`['Jews', 'Jews', 'Judaism.', 'Judaism.', 'Jews']`.

The visible duplication is display-only -- `get_or_create(heading=...)`
collapses equal headings and the through table has a unique index, so no
duplicate rows exist. The real defect is underneath it: two distinct
headings are both stored as the broad subject `Jews`. The intended form
joins subdivisions with " -- ", as `load_test_data.py:284-289` shows
("Talmud -- Commentaries").

Fix by assembling the heading from `$a` plus subdivisions and deduping
on a normalized key, in `sources/marc.py`. `_attach_from_candidate` is
the single writer for all three ingest paths, so one fix covers
everything. Deduping in the template would hide the symptom and keep
storing the wrong subject.

Existing tests stay green (`tests/test_marc.py:282-284` covers 650s that
carry only `$a`). Add a case with a subdivided 650 plus a duplicate FAST
650, and an e2e assertion that the confirm page lists each subject once.

The 8 existing Subject rows were written under the truncating logic; a
backfill would need the original MARC, and no stored record has
`source_marc` populated yet.

title: Staged images keep a .png suffix over JPEG bytes
description:
`staging_image_path` in `ingest/models.py` allows `.png` through
`JPEG_SUFFIXES`, but the capture form re-encodes every selection to
`image/jpeg` while preserving the original filename.

Pick a PNG screenshot of a title page and it is stored at
`staging/.../<hex>.png` holding JPEG bytes, and served as
`Content-Type: image/png`. Browsers sniff past it; anything trusting the
extension or MIME type does not.

Given the unconditional re-encode, the suffix should normalise to `.jpg`
for anything that is not already `.jpg`/`.jpeg`. The docstring already
explains the re-encode, so this is a one-line change plus a test.

Found in review of PR #7.
close_reason: Merged in PR #17

title: Treat an incoming record as evidence about a set, not its definition
description:
Multipart works — a Shas, a Mishnah with commentary, a multi-volume Shulḥan ʻarukh, a monographic series — arrive from source catalogs in at least five incompatible treatments. otzar reads one of them.

The variation is not error and will not converge. It reflects real differences in cataloging rules, local practice, and era, and multiple catalogers have confirmed it is what to expect. A design that treats one treatment as correct and the others as malformed will keep losing sets.

Today `detect_series_from_marc` reads 490/830 and whatever it finds becomes the `Series`. A record catalogued as a multipart monograph, linked only by uniform title, or analytic to a host record forms no set at all.

Invert the relationship. otzar holds its own opinion of what a set is, which volumes belong to it, and what order they sit in. Each incoming record is one witness to that opinion. Copy cataloging supplies evidence; it does not get to define, split, or silently overwrite a set.

## Two goals that pull in different directions

**Finding** records across differing practice — maximize recall. Read every field that could carry set membership, in every treatment, and use all of it for search and candidate scoring.

**Holding** records consistently once found — maximize consistency. One set, one identity, one ordering, stable across imports and correctable by hand.

The first is permissive, the second is opinionated, and collapsing them is the mistake to avoid. A field can be excellent evidence for finding and useless for identity: a transcribed 490 is exactly that.

## Why it matters for this catalog

The target collections are large sets of Gemara and commentary, held by people who are not catalogers. If a twenty-volume Shas lands as twenty unrelated records, or as one set holding one volume with nineteen dropped, the catalog has failed at its main job. "What do we have of Berakhot" is the question being asked.

## Sequence

The children are ordered. Reading more fields (1) is what makes the identity work (3) possible, and the authorized-form preference (2) is the rule identity applies. Manual correction (4) is what makes the result trustworthy, and is the child that decides whether the epic delivers — everything upstream is recall, and that one is the consistency. The lookup helper (otzar-zx8) and the documentation come last because both describe behaviour that has to exist first.

## Not in scope

Holdings-level enumeration (853/863/866). otzar reads bibliographic records over SRU and does not see holdings. Authority file maintenance. Becoming a cataloging tool: otzar consumes copy cataloging, it does not produce it.

title: Read the fields that carry set membership beyond 490 and 830
description:
`sources/marc.py` reads fifteen tags: 008, 010, 020, 035, 050, 082, 100, 245, 260, 264, 490, 650, 700, 830, 880. Set detection uses two of them.

Of the ways a multipart work actually arrives, otzar sees one:

| Treatment | What carries the set | Read today |
|---|---|---|
| Series treatment | `490 $a $v`, `830 $a $v` | yes |
| Series statement, pre-2008 | `440 $a $v` | no |
| Multipart monograph | `245 $a` plus `$n` part number, `$p` part title | parsed, unused |
| Uniform title | `130` / `240` — `Talmud. $p Berakhot.` | no |
| Analytic | `773` host item entry | no |
| Set record with contents | `505` enhanced, `$t` per volume | no |
| Named series added entry | `800` / `810` / `811` | no |
| Volume enumeration on a set record | `020 $q`, `300 $a` | no |
| Series ISSN | `490 $x`, `830 $x`, `800`/`810`/`811 $x`, `440 $x` | no |
| Host item ISSN | `773 $x` | no |

## What to add, in order of value for this collection

The order below is measured rather than reasoned. A survey of 1,027 records from NLI, LC and DNB, written up in `docs/marc-in-practice.md`, counted how often each treatment actually appears in the multi-volume Judaica this catalog exists to hold, split by era of publication. Three fields a reading of the format ranks highly turned out to be near-absent, and two that the format does not obviously flag turned out to be the most common signals present.

**`130` and `240`, uniform title. 42 and 20 records of 122.** The highest-value addition, and the survey confirms it. For rabbinic and liturgical texts the uniform title is authority-controlled and exists precisely to collocate a work across varying transcriptions — `Talmud Bavli. $p Pesahim` holds whether the piece reads Talmud Bavli, Gemara, or Masekhet Berakhot, and whether it was romanized under ALA-LC or something older. `130` is the main entry form, used when there is no 1XX author, which is the normal case for Talmud and Mishnah; `240` is the form used when a 1XX is present.

`$p` is where the volume identity lives, and it is usually a name rather than a number: Pesahim, Rosh ha-shanah, פרה. `130 $p`, `240 $p` and `730 $p` together appear on more records than every numeric volume designation in the corpus combined.

**`730`, added entry uniform title. 45 records.** The most common set-bearing field after the title itself, and the survey's biggest surprise. It has the same name-title structure as `130` and names the works a volume contains, which is how a compilation says what is inside it: `730 0# $a תלמוד בבלי. $p סוכה. $k לקוטים`. `700 $t` and `710 $t` are the name-title forms of the same idea.

**`246`, varying form of title. 54% of NLI records, 14% of LC.** Largely an NLI habit rather than a general one, and the reason is that NLI uses it to carry the cross-script variant: `246 1# $i בשער גם: $a ערוך השלחן` against a romanized `245`. Reading `245` alone concludes the record has one script.

**`773`, host item entry. 11% of pre-1945 records, 19% after 1990.** The analytic's pointer at its host record. `$t` carries the host title and `$g` the part designation — except where it carries neither: fifteen records link by `$w` control number alone, eleven of them pre-1945. A reader expecting `$t` finds nothing.

**`020 $q`, volume qualifier, and the ISBN problem behind it. Absent entirely before 1945 — 0 of 279 records carry any `020` at all.** For the older half of a collection there is no ISBN to qualify, and no barcode path either. Where an ISBN does exist, the qualifier is not reliably in `$q`: NLI writes it inline in `$a` as `9780827609426 (v. [1])`. Where one bibliographic record covers a set, the enumeration lives in the ISBN qualifier and the extent statement rather than in any series field. otzar-4x2 has the worked case, the Sapirstein Rashi record, and the two Commentators' Bible records already in the catalog show the same ISBN qualified as a volume by NLI and unqualified by LC.

**`$x`, the series ISSN. One record.** The only assigned identifier anywhere in the set problem, and near-absent from this material, because ISSN is assigned to continuing resources: a monographic series carries one, a multipart monograph does not. High precision, near-zero recall. Decisive for deciding which set a record belongs to, worthless as a filter, and never something to require. `022 $a` covers the case where the catalogued thing is itself the serial; `$y` is an incorrect ISSN and `$z` a cancelled one, both worth keeping as variant evidence and neither fit to establish identity.

**`505`, contents note. 185 records, six of them structured, none before 1945.** A set record enumerating its own volumes. The other 179 put everything in a single `$a`, often an unpunctuated list of contained works. A parser written for `$t` addresses one record. The blob form is a separate and harder problem, and worth deferring rather than pretending the structured case is the common one.

**`440`, obsolete series statement. 0% before 1945, 3% between 1945 and 1989, 0% after 1990.** The expectation that older copy is full of it has the shape of the argument right and the era wrong: 440 was valid from the late 1960s until 2008, so the records carrying it are the ones catalogued inside that window and never reconverted. Genuinely old copy does not use it, because it predates the field. Cheap to read and cheap to skip.

**`245 $n` and `$p`. One record.** Both are already parsed into `volume_part_number` and `volume_part_title` and then ignored for set-forming, so reading them is nearly free. The pattern is real but rare compared with the uniform title, which expresses the same thing in `130 $p` or `730 $p`.

**`800`, `810`, `811`, series added entry under a name. Zero records in 1,027**, across three catalogs and three eras. A set entered under a person or corporate body is a real MARC treatment and is not one these endpoints send for this material. Worth knowing about; not worth building for on this evidence.

## Shape of the output

`$x` does not mean the same thing in every field. In 6XX it is a general topical subdivision and `_HEADING_CODES = frozenset("avxyz")` in `sources/marc.py` treats it as part of the heading. In 4XX and 8XX it is the ISSN. Reusing that frozenset for series extraction would append an ISSN to the series title and produce a title form that matches nothing.

Emit these as separate, labelled pieces of evidence rather than flattening them into `series_title` and `series_volume`. The identity work downstream has to weigh an authorized form above a transcribed one, and cannot do that once both have been collapsed into one key.

## Tests

One record per treatment, drawn from real NLI, LC and DNB output where possible rather than hand-built MARC — the point of the ticket is that real practice varies more than a fixture author imagines. LCCN 2001531851 is a good starting fixture: it exercises four of these at once.

title: Prefer the authorized series form over the transcribed one for identity
description:
`sources/marc.py` reads `490 $a` and falls back to `830 $a` only when 490 is absent, and does the same for `$v`. That preference is backwards for deciding which set a record belongs to.

490 is transcribed: whatever was printed on the piece in hand, with that volume's punctuation, that volume's spelling, and no normalization. 830 is the authorized form, established by the cataloger for the express purpose of making variant transcriptions of one set collocate. For identity, 830 should win. Same for the volume designation.

Keep both. The transcribed form is what appears on the physical volume a user is holding, so it belongs in search and in display; it is only unfit to be the identity key.

## The indicator says which to expect

`490` first indicator 0 means the series is not traced — no 8XX added entry exists, and the transcribed form is all there is. First indicator 1 means it is traced, and an 800/810/811/830 carries the authorized form. That indicator is the signal for whether an authorized form should be looked for, and is worth reading rather than inferring from whether an 830 happens to be present.

## Scope

The preference order, the indicator handling, and keeping the transcribed form available alongside rather than discarding it. The larger question of how competing evidence is weighed belongs to the identity work; this is the one rule that is unambiguous on its own.
close_reason: done

title: Give a set an identity of its own, separate from any record's claim about it
description:
A `Series` is currently identified by its normalized title alone and created on demand from whatever a confirmed record's 490 or 830 said. Three consequences follow, and all three are visible in a real collection:

- Two records transcribing the set differently split it into two rows.
- Two unrelated sets sharing a generic title merge into one.
- A set has no existence until some record names it, so there is nothing to attach a volume to before the first one arrives.

What is wanted instead is a `Series` that persists in its own right, carries the authorized form when one is known plus the variant forms that have been seen, and is matched against by accumulated evidence rather than conjured from a single field.

## Matching order

ISSN first, then uniform title, then authorized series title, then normalized transcribed title, then part-title structure from `245 $a` where `$n` or `$p` is present. Each is weaker than the one before, and the weaker ones should be able to attach a record to an existing set without being able to create a new one on their own — a bare transcribed title that matches nothing is a weak reason to declare a new set exists. An ISSN match is strong enough to do both.

ISSN sits above uniform title because it is the only rung that is an identifier rather than a string comparison. Every other rung compares a form one cataloger typed against a form another cataloger typed, and the whole difficulty of this ticket is that those forms vary legitimately. An ISSN is issued to the series precisely so they collocate. Its coverage is narrow — continuing resources have one, multipart monographs do not — so it will be absent far more often than present, and that costs nothing: a ladder is allowed to have a rung most records skip.

## Where identifiers live

`ExternalIdentifier` has a foreign key to `Record` and nothing else, so an identifier can only ever describe a record. That is already wrong for the identifiers otzar holds: the model declares a `VIAF` type that nothing writes, because a VIAF ID names an author, and `Author.viaf_id` exists as a separate column to work around it. `NLI` is declared and unwritten for the same reason. A series ISSN has the same shape — it names the set, not the volume in hand — so hanging it off `Record` would repeat the mistake a third time.

Generalize the model: nullable foreign keys to `record`, `series` and `author`, with a `CheckConstraint` that exactly one is set. One rule, one sentence — an identifier names exactly one entity.

The alternatives are worse for this codebase. A `GenericForeignKey` gives up referential integrity and cascade behaviour, and prefetching across it on SQLite is slower for no gain at three owner types. Per-owner tables repeat the same four columns three times, which is the internal-consistency test failing outright.

Folding `Author.viaf_id` into the generalized table is the natural consequence and is tracked separately, because it reaches into the authority and enrichment code and would otherwise inflate this ticket past reviewing.

Worth noting while here: `LCC` and `DDC` are classifications, not identifiers. They locate a work in a hierarchy rather than naming it, and two different works can share one. They are not wrong to store, but they are the reason the table's name will keep reading slightly false.

## Evidence belongs on the link, not on the series

The `490` first indicator says whether the series is traced: `0` means no 8XX exists and the transcribed form is all there is, `1` means an authorized form is out there to be found. `bd-tz2s.2` covers reading it. This ticket decides where it goes, and the answer is not on `Series`.

One record can trace a series and another can leave it untraced. That is a fact about each record's cataloguing, not about the set, and storing it on `Series` flattens two records' disagreement into one value — losing exactly the distinction this epic exists to keep. The same holds for the transcribed `490 $a` that `bd-tz2s.2` wants preserved alongside the authorized form: it is what was printed on one volume, so it is evidence from one record.

Both want the same home: the link between a record and a series. `SeriesVolume` is the only thing resembling that link today, and it is currently about position rather than about evidence. Deciding whether membership evidence gets a model of its own, or whether `SeriesVolume` grows into one, is part of this ticket.

## Absorbs bd-1s79

`SeriesVolume` declares `unique_together = ("series", "volume_number")` on a non-null `CharField`, so the empty string behaves as a position exactly one record per series can hold, and an unnumbered set holds one volume while the rest are logged and dropped. The narrow fix is a nullable column and a `UniqueConstraint` conditioned on the designation existing.

Do it here rather than ahead of this work. Landing it first means a migration this ticket immediately migrates again, and the question of what a volume's position means when no source supplied one is the same question this ticket is answering.

## What position means

Three cases have to be distinguishable, and today they are not:

- A volume with a designation from the source: `v. 3`, `חלק ג`, `vol. III` — all position 3.
- A volume known to belong to the set with no designation anywhere: it has membership but no position.
- A gap: a position known to exist, from a `505` or from a numbering run, with no record held. `create_series_volumes` already builds these.

`SeriesVolume.Meta.ordering` is `["volume_number"]`, so undesignated volumes will collect at one end of the list. The series page has to say what they are rather than showing a blank cell.

title: Let a person fix set membership and order, and keep the fix
description:
No parser gets a Shas right across five cataloging eras. Whatever the evidence-weighing does, some sets will come out wrong, and the catalog needs a way for a person to say "these records are one set, in this order" and have it hold.

The requirement that makes this real: a human assertion outranks imported evidence permanently. The next record confirmed into the catalog must not be able to reorder an asserted sequence, move a record out of a set someone placed it in, or split a set someone merged.

## What that implies

Each membership and each position carries where it came from — imported or asserted. Import logic reads that marker and declines to downgrade. This is the same shape as the provenance already recorded on records, and should follow it rather than inventing a second vocabulary.

Both mistakes need an undo, because both will happen: merging two `Series` rows that are one set, and splitting one row that turned out to be two. Merge has to carry volumes and their positions across, and has to have an answer for two records claiming the same position after the merge.

Ordering has to be settable by hand independent of any designation, because a set can be conventionally ordered without being numbered — tractates of a Shas run in a traditional order that no `$v` states.

## Why this one decides the epic

Everything upstream of this ticket improves recall: more fields read, better evidence, better matching. This is the ticket that turns the result into something a person can rely on, because it is the only one that guarantees a correct answer stays correct. A catalog that re-breaks a set every time a new volume is confirmed is worse than one that never grouped them, because the user stops trusting the grouping.

title: Document how otzar handles sets and volumes
description:
Write the set-and-volume model down in the user documentation, for a reader who knows cataloging. The bar: an experienced cataloger reads it and says "yes, that makes sense for this app" — not "that is just how MARC works," and not "that is wrong."

That reader is worth writing for even though they are not the primary user. They are the person a collection owner will ask when something looks off, and they are the person who will notice if otzar's model quietly contradicts the records it ingested.

## What it has to cover

**What varies in the wild, named in MARC terms and without ranking.** The treatments a multipart work arrives in — series added entry, multipart monograph with `245 $n`/`$p`, uniform title, analytic with `773`, set record with a `505` contents note — described as legitimate alternatives reflecting different rules and eras. State plainly that otzar expects the variation rather than treating one form as correct.

**What otzar reads from each, and what it does with what it reads.** Field by field. A cataloger should be able to predict, from a record they are looking at, what otzar will make of it.

**The split between finding and holding.** Why every signal is used for search and candidate scoring, while only some are allowed to establish identity. The worked case is the transcribed `490`: good evidence that a record is a candidate, unfit to decide which set it belongs to, because it carries one volume's punctuation and spelling rather than the set's established form. This is the paragraph the whole document turns on.

**How set signals affect candidate scoring, and what they deliberately do not do.** A series match raising a candidate is useful; a series match rescuing a candidate whose title does not match is not. Say where the ceiling is and why.

**otzar's own model.** `Series`, `SeriesVolume`, position, membership, and gap placeholders. What a position means, what it means for a volume to have membership but no position, and how volumes with no designation are ordered and displayed. Where otzar's model deliberately does not mirror MARC, say so and say why.

**What happens on re-ingest, and what a person's correction outranks.** The guarantee is the point: a set someone has fixed by hand stays fixed. Spell out what "asserted" beats and what it does not.

**What otzar does not do.** No holdings enumeration — it reads bibliographic records over SRU, not `853`/`863`/`866`. No authority file maintenance. No attempt to be a cataloging tool. Naming the boundaries is what earns the cataloger's trust in the rest.

**A worked example.** One set — a Shas is the natural choice — arriving three different ways from three catalogs and landing in one series with volumes in one order. Show the actual fields in each incoming record and the resulting rows. This does more than the prose to make the model legible.

## Where it goes

Probably its own page rather than a section of `docs/user-guide.md`: the guide is task-oriented and this is a model explanation, and the audience is partly different. Decide when writing.

## When

After the model settles. This documents behaviour, and documenting it before the identity and correction work lands means writing it twice.

title: Configure logging so the application's log calls do something
description:
`otzar/settings.py` has no `LOGGING` setting, so Django's defaults apply and the application's own loggers get nothing. Verified rather than inferred: the root logger has no handlers and sits at `WARNING`, and every module logger inherits that.

Two consequences.
